Report exact-label accuracy with bootstrap CIs on 500 real test items for each of the six configurations and for spec-prompted zero-shot Qwen3-0.6B, together with the gap between the paper's setting (alpha 16, T=100) and the best longer or higher-alpha run.

follow_ups.title: Length and compositional generalization of a compiled instruction-to-action-DSL function
follow_ups.question: The paper's Avatar Director program produced the expected action structure for 43 of 44 hand-authored instructions. Does a compiled 0.6B function that maps instructions to an action DSL remain parseable and exact as instructions grow longer or combine constructs beyond what its synthetic training data contains?
follow_ups.method: Define a small action DSL (about 12 verbs; steps separated by ';'; repetition 'verb xN'; durations 'verb@Ns'; parallel 'a+b' only for allowed pairs) with a Python parser and canonical form, write a spec describing it, and synthesize 2,400 instruction-to-program pairs with Qwen3-8B (thinking disabled, the paper's Appendix D prompt, unparseable outputs dropped). Compile two Qwen3-0.6B LoRAs with the paper's recipe (r=64, alpha=16, lr 2e-4, batch 48, 100 cosine steps, standard LoRA init with B=0): one on all valid pairs and one only on pairs with at most 3 steps. Evaluate on 600 Python-generated test items (100 random programs for each length 1 to 6, verbalized with several paraphrase templates) by parse validity and exact canonical-program match, broken down by length and construct; compare against Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-8B prompted with the spec, and report the step-count distribution of the training pairs.

follow_ups.title: Modular pipeline of compiled functions vs. one monolithic compiled function for composite specifications
follow_ups.question: The paper argues that compiled functions compose with ordinary code but supports this only with deployed demos. At equal teacher data and training compute, does routing between separately compiled sub-functions beat compiling the whole composite specification as one function? Do module errors compound as stage accuracies predict?
follow_ups.method: Build two composite tasks with gold labels from public data: (i) a mix of AG News snippets and SST-2 sentences with the spec 'if a news snippet, output its topic; if a movie review, output its sentiment', and (ii) Emotion texts with the spec 'output POSITIVE for joy, love or surprise, otherwise output sadness, anger or fear'. For each, use Qwen3-8B synthesis (thinking disabled, the paper's Appendix D prompt) and the paper's LoRA recipe on frozen Qwen3-0.6B (r=64, alpha=16, lr 2e-4, batch 48, standard LoRA init with B=0) to compile two systems: a router plus sub-function adapters composed in Python (2,400 pairs and 100 steps per module), and a monolithic adapter from the full spec, trained both at the default budget (2,400 pairs, 100 steps) and at a budget matched to the modular pipeline's total pairs and steps. On 500 held-out test items per composite, report end-to-end accuracy and macro-F1, router and per-module accuracy, and modular accuracy versus the product of stage accuracies.

follow_ups.title: Separate adapter training from the run-time scaffold
follow_ups.question: For paper-style functions, how much do adapter training and the compiler-generated scaffold each contribute to accuracy?
follow_ups.method: Construct 128 oracle-labeled training and 128 held-out examples per task for ordered arxiv /pdf/ identifier extraction that ignores /abs/ links, and IMMEDIATE-versus-WAIT triage of unambiguous action/deadline emails versus newsletters/FYI messages; have non-thinking Qwen3-4B generate a scaffold of at most 128 tokens from each specification and two training examples. Run a two-by-two comparison of literal specification versus scaffold and frozen versus LoRA-adapted Qwen3-0.6B, using non-thinking mode, standard zero-update adapter initialization, rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 60 steps, maximum sequence length 384, and two matched seeds. Report oracle accuracy, formatting failures, paired test-set intervals, and seed variation for the main effects and interaction, without treating the frozen baseline as PAW's amortized compiler.

follow_ups.title: JSON validation versus semantic supervision repair
follow_ups.question: Does repairing teacher-label errors improve compiled functions beyond merely rejecting malformed JSON?
follow_ups.method: Generate 256 training inputs containing canonical arxiv /pdf/ and /abs/ links, repeated identifiers, and irrelevant text, plus 256 held-out inputs with disjoint identifiers; require extraction of /pdf/ identifiers as a JSON array preserving encounter order and duplicates, and ask non-thinking Qwen3-4B for input-output pairs in the paper's JSON schema. Keep the same structurally accepted inputs in two corpora, retaining teacher labels in one and replacing them with executable-oracle labels in the other, then train non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B adapters with rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 100 steps, sequence length 384, and two matched seeds. Report structural rejection rates, semantic error rates among accepted teacher labels, and paired held-out accuracy differences with intervals, allowing a small or uncertain repair effect if teacher errors are rare.

follow_ups.title: Controlled small-and-large open-teacher mixtures
follow_ups.question: Does a two-to-one teacher mixture help after input diversity and student training exposure are controlled?
follow_ups.method: For each of ordered /pdf/-only arxiv extraction and unambiguous action/deadline-versus-newsletter/FYI email triage, generate 192 training inputs and 128 oracle-labeled held-out inputs, and obtain labels for every training input from both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B with thinking disabled. Train non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B on small-teacher-only, large-teacher-only, and mixed corpora containing 128 small-teacher and 64 large-teacher labels on exactly the same inputs, using new rank-64, alpha-16 adapters, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 60 steps, sequence length 384, and two matched seeds. Measure each teacher's oracle accuracy and complementary correct predictions, then report student accuracy differences, paired intervals, seed variation, and measured labeling time rather than assuming the open-teacher mixture reproduces the hosted-teacher result.

follow_ups.title: Unique supervision versus repetition at fixed updates
follow_ups.question: Do additional unique examples help beyond repeatedly training on a smaller corpus?
follow_ups.method: Create nested sets of 32, 128, and 512 oracle-labeled arxiv extraction examples, balanced across eight input-template families and matched link-count distributions, with /pdf/ identifiers returned in order and /abs/ links ignored; reserve 512 tests with disjoint identifiers and unseen combinations of link types and positions. Train non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B from standard LoRA initialization at each dataset size using rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 16, 64 steps, sequence length 256, and two seeds, giving every condition exactly 1024 example exposures through repetition. Compare training loss, held-out oracle accuracy, and error types with paired test-set intervals and seed variation, distinguishing an imprecise plateau from evidence of negligible benefit.

follow_ups.title: Warm starts under specification revisions
follow_ups.question: Does reusing a compiled adapter accelerate recompilation, or preserve obsolete behavior after a rule changes?
follow_ups.method: Generate oracle-labeled arxiv extraction datasets with 128 training and 256 identifier-disjoint test inputs for an original /pdf/-only specification and two revisions: extracting both /pdf/ and /abs/ identifiers, and extracting only /abs/ identifiers. For two seeds, train a non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B parent adapter and then compare copied-parent versus standard zero-update initialization for each revision, using the revised specification in every prompt and rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 60 steps, sequence length 384, with evaluation at steps 0, 15, 30, and 60. Report accuracy-versus-training-time curves, errors specifically consistent with the obsolete rule, and the separately measured parent-build cost; this tests artifact reuse rather than PAW's hypernetwork initialization.

follow_ups.title: Synthetic coverage and distribution shift
follow_ups.question: Can targeted synthesis improve robustness beyond a generic request for diverse examples?
follow_ups.method: Have non-thinking Qwen3-4B synthesize ordered /pdf/-only arxiv extraction pairs using either the paper's generic diversity request or that request augmented with mixed /pdf/-/abs/ lists, repeated identifiers, and non-arxiv distractors, generating at most 256 candidates per condition and retaining up to 128 length-matched valid inputs per condition. Replace both corpora's labels with the same executable oracle to isolate coverage from labeling errors, then train non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B with rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 60 steps, sequence length 384, and two matched seeds. Evaluate 256 identifier-disjoint cases evenly divided among clean inputs, unfamiliar surrounding prose, four-to-six-link inputs, and misleading link distractors, reporting stratum-specific accuracy and paired intervals rather than only an aggregate score.

follow_ups.title: Error propagation through a composed program tree
follow_ups.question: Does a small composed application fail mainly at routing or inside its task-specific compiled functions?
follow_ups.method: Generate requests asking either for ordered /pdf/-only arxiv identifier extraction or for IMMEDIATE-versus-WAIT triage of unambiguous action/deadline emails versus newsletters/FYI messages, with executable labels for the router and both child functions, 128 training examples per program, and 256 held-out requests with disjoint identifiers and templates. Independently train three non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B adapters using rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 60 steps, sequence length 384, and two seeds, then use ordinary code to dispatch according to the router's PDF or TRIAGE output. Measure standalone and actual end-to-end accuracy, invalid routes, and joint failures, and run oracle-routing and oracle-child-output interventions that preserve the other learned stage rather than approximating reliability by multiplying component accuracies.

follow_ups.title: Syntax validation versus action correctness
follow_ups.question: How often does a DSL validator accept an executable but incorrect action program, and does retrying rejected outputs help?
follow_ups.method: Generate 256 training and 256 held-out natural-language commands using jump, wave, dance, and sit_proud, ordered sequences, and one-to-three repetitions; define a small DSL with one primitive action per line, expand repetitions programmatically, and keep reference programs within twelve actions while withholding test paraphrases and longer combinations. Evaluate frozen and LoRA-adapted non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B, training rank-64, alpha-16 adapters with learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 60 steps, sequence length 384, two seeds, and a 64-token generation limit. Compare unchecked execution, a whitelist-and-one-to-twelve-line validator with abstention, and one same-model retry receiving only parser errors after rejection, reporting unconditional semantic success, acceptance coverage, and valid-but-wrong rates with intervals.

follow_ups.title: Oracle-calibrated local LEM judging
follow_ups.question: How accurately can an allowed local model implement LEM, especially when formatting rules and substantive errors differ?
follow_ups.method: Construct 64 arxiv extraction cases containing two distinct /pdf/ identifiers and an /abs/ distractor, with half the specifications requiring a JSON array and half permitting any ordered list, then make six outputs per case: canonical, whitespace-varied, alternate-container, wrong-identifier, omission, and reversed-order versions with correctness determined programmatically. Obtain non-thinking Qwen3-4B judgments using Appendix E's LEM prompt on these 384 randomized cases, and additionally judge 128 frozen Qwen3-0.6B predictions under strict-JSON specifications against the extraction oracle, limiting judge completions to 96 tokens. Report false-positive and false-negative rates, agreement, and binomial intervals by error and formatting category, alongside malformed-judgment rates, without assuming this local judge inherits the paper's GPT-5.5 validation.

follow_ups.title: Quantized execution and local compilation amortization
follow_ups.question: How does runtime quantization change function accuracy, latency, memory use, and the call count needed to amortize compilation?
follow_ups.method: Use non-thinking Qwen3-4B to label 192 generated arxiv inputs for ordered /pdf/-only identifier extraction, then train one non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B adapter with rank 64, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, batch 8, 100 steps, and sequence length 384, recording synthesis and training time separately and reserving 256 oracle-labeled, identifier-disjoint tests. Reload the same adapter separately on BF16, 8-bit, and 4-bit NF4 interpreters, evaluate all tests with a 64-token output limit, and benchmark identical subsets against direct Qwen3-4B execution at batch sizes 1 and 16 using CUDA-synchronized timing. Report oracle accuracy, throughput, median and tail latency, peak GPU memory, and one-time model/artifact loading costs, calculating a local wall-time crossover only when the student has a measured per-call advantage and keeping accuracy differences explicit.

follow_ups.title: Does task-specific training beat specification-only prompting?
follow_ups.question: On rule-checkable functions drawn from the paper's examples, does a trained adapter improve held-out behavior over the same frozen interpreter with only the specification prompt?
follow_ups.method: Because the supplied paper reports FuzzyBench-Hard summary scores but does not include its examples, build a seeded, oracle-checked proxy from its two concrete tasks: extract arXiv IDs from `/pdf/` URLs while ignoring `/abs/` links, and triage templated emails as `immediate` for an explicit action or deadline by EOD versus `wait` for FYI/newsletters; make 64 training and 100 held-out examples per task with disjoint wording templates. Train three seeded rank-16 LoRAs per task on Qwen3-0.6B for 100 steps and compare greedy predictions with the frozen model under the identical specification prompt, using a deterministic semantic scorer and paired per-task intervals.

follow_ups.title: Local teacher-mixture ablation
follow_ups.question: Does mixing supervision from different local teacher models improve a compiled function over using either teacher alone?
follow_ups.method: Use local Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B as small and large teacher proxies, not as replications of the paper's hosted teachers, to label the same 128 programmatically generated inputs for the `/pdf/`-ID extractor with a fixed JSON prompt; retry malformed JSON only, retain valid but incorrect labels, and measure each teacher's error against the oracle. Train three Qwen3-0.6B rank-16 adapters for 100 identical steps on small-teacher, large-teacher, or fixed 1:1 mixed labels, then compare semantic accuracy on 200 rule-labeled held-out URLs.

follow_ups.title: Unique-example scaling at fixed optimization budget
follow_ups.question: When the number of optimizer steps is fixed, how does the number of unique supervision pairs affect generalization?
follow_ups.method: Generate 32, 128, and 512 unique oracle-labeled pairs for the `/pdf/` extractor, plus 200 held-out URLs with unseen combinations of valid `/pdf/` and ignored `/abs/` links; train separate rank-16 Qwen3-0.6B adapters for 100 steps at batch size 8, sampling with replacement so every condition sees exactly 800 pair presentations. Repeat each size with three seeds and report held-out semantic accuracy and its range, isolating unique-example coverage from optimizer-step count.

follow_ups.title: Sensitivity to controlled supervision errors
follow_ups.question: How does the compiled function's accuracy change as the fraction of incorrect but valid training labels increases?
follow_ups.method: Programmatically generate 256 training and 200 held-out email messages for the paper's action/deadline-versus-FYI triage rule, using non-overlapping wording templates; create matched training labels with 0%, 10%, or 25% of targets flipped to the other valid class, using three seeded nested masks. Train rank-16 Qwen3-0.6B adapters for 100 steps per mask and condition, then score only against clean held-out oracle labels and report accuracy by noise level and mask.

follow_ups.title: Does the run-time scaffold carry behavior beyond the adapter?
follow_ups.question: How much does a compiled function depend on its packaged specification and examples at run time?
follow_ups.method: Train a rank-16 Qwen3-0.6B adapter for the `/pdf/` extractor on 64 oracle pairs using a run-time scaffold with the full specification and four correct demonstrations that are disjoint from the training and test data. On the same 200 held-out URLs, compare greedy semantic accuracy for the trained adapter with the full scaffold, the specification alone, and a task-agnostic input/output wrapper, and also score the frozen base with the full scaffold.

follow_ups.title: Transfer warm start as a proxy for amortized initialization
follow_ups.question: Does a related-function adapter warm start reduce target-specific training steps enough to justify its one-time cost?
follow_ups.method: Because the supplied paper does not provide the PAW initializer weights, use a transparent transfer proxy: train a rank-16 Qwen3-0.6B LoRA for 100 steps on 64 oracle examples apiece from email triage, a small wave/jump/dance action DSL, and `/abs/`-ID extraction, then use it to initialize the paper's `/pdf/`-only extractor. Compare this warm start with a fresh LoRA using the same 64 target pairs and scaffold after 10, 30, and 100 target steps on 200 held-out URLs, reporting accuracy-versus-steps and the one-time warm-start training cost separately.

follow_ups.title: Rule-oracle validation of a local semantic judge
follow_ups.question: Can a local open-model judge recognize valid output variations that exact string matching rejects, without human labels?
follow_ups.method: Construct 128 rule-labeled specification/input/reference/candidate cases from the paper's identifier-extraction and email-triage tasks: 64 candidates are semantically valid whitespace or container variations allowed by their specifications, and 64 contain substantive errors such as missing or extra IDs or a wrong triage label. Prompt local Qwen3-0.6B with the paper's Appendix E LEM rules, treat malformed JSON as a wrong judgment, and compare its decisions with the programmatic oracle and exact-string match using accuracy, false-positive and false-negative rates, and Cohen's kappa.

follow_ups.title: Streaming compilation under controlled teacher delays
follow_ups.question: When supervision arrives gradually, does overlapping training with synthesis reduce compile time without changing the accepted examples?
follow_ups.method: Preload Qwen3-0.6B outside the timing window and use a deterministic teacher stub that releases 64 oracle-labeled URL-extraction pairs in four ordered 16-example chunks at 0, 5, 10, and 15 seconds; compare a build that waits for all chunks with one that starts training each chunk as it arrives. Both builds train the same rank-16 LoRA for 10 steps per chunk in the same order, for 40 steps total, and are repeated three times; measure end-to-end time, trainer data-wait time, and held-out accuracy, treating delays as simulated rather than real teacher latency.

follow_ups.title: Composed program tree versus one function
follow_ups.question: Does composing independently compiled decisions preserve correctness compared with a single end-to-end function?
follow_ups.method: Create 256 training and 200 held-out synthetic website-helper records with site/page context, a link, course and forum snippets, and a question whose oracle action is `LINK`, `COURSE`, `FORUM`, or `BOTH`; train a two-node Qwen3-0.6B tree with a rank-8 LINK-versus-answer router followed by a rank-8 source selector, while deterministic code looks up or merges the selected content. Compare it with one rank-16 adapter predicting the same four-way action, matching total LoRA rank and 100 optimizer steps (50 per tree node, 100 for the single function), and report decision accuracy, exact returned-content correctness, and which tree node causes failures.

follow_ups.title: Offline portability of a compiled action DSL
follow_ups.question: Can a compiled function generate executable action programs for unseen combinations and run from a packaged artifact without network access?
follow_ups.method: Define a small motion DSL using the paper's sequence, repetition, and duration constructs over `wave`, `jump`, `dance`, and `sit_proudly`; generate 128 oracle instruction/program pairs and 100 held-out combinations with familiar primitives in unseen orders, then train a rank-16 Qwen3-0.6B LoRA for 100 steps. Package the adapter, specification/scaffold, and interpreter metadata in a `.paw`-style artifact, then reload it in a fresh process after caching the base model and blocking outbound network access; pass greedy outputs through a deterministic parser and report exact AST accuracy, syntax acceptance, pre/post-reload agreement, artifact size, and median local latency.

follow_ups.title: Compile-by-training vs frozen-interpreter prompting
follow_ups.question: Does training a LoRA adapter on teacher-synthesized examples improve correctness over prompting the frozen interpreter with the same specification?
follow_ups.method: For 3 specs drawn from the paper (email triage immediate versus wait, arXiv /pdf/ ID extraction ignoring /abs/, and link-versus-answer routing), use Qwen3-8B with the Appendix D JSON prompt to synthesize about 300 input-output pairs per spec and hold out 50 for testing. Train a Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapter (rank 64, alpha 16, about 60 steps, batch 16) per spec and compare it to frozen Qwen3-0.6B with a scaffold prompt encoding the spec, scoring both with rule-based checks and a Qwen3-8B judge using the Appendix E LEM prompt.

follow_ups.title: Mixed larger-teacher supervision vs small-teacher-only
follow_ups.question: Does mixing examples from a larger open teacher with a cheaper small teacher improve accuracy compared to small-teacher-only supervision at fixed data size?
follow_ups.method: For 2 specs (email triage and arXiv extraction), generate 300 unique pairs per spec in two conditions: 300 from Qwen3-0.6B versus 200 from Qwen3-0.6B plus 100 from Qwen3-8B, using the same Appendix D prompt and JSON validation. Train Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters identically (rank 64, about 60 steps) on each condition and compare held-out accuracy using rule-based scoring and a Qwen3-8B LEM judge.

follow_ups.title: Unique-pair data scaling
follow_ups.question: Does increasing the number of unique teacher-synthesized pairs improve compiled-function accuracy under fixed optimization?
follow_ups.method: For 2 paper specs, synthesize 100, 300, and 600 unique pairs with Qwen3-8B and train separate Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters (rank 64, fixed about 60 steps, batch 16) on each size. Evaluate all adapters on the same 50 held-out inputs per spec with rule-based and Qwen3-8B LEM scoring to measure the scaling curve.

follow_ups.title: Open-model LEM vs exact match on cosmetic variants
follow_ups.question: Does an open-model LEM judge tolerate cosmetic formatting differences while rejecting substantive errors where string exact match fails?
follow_ups.method: Build about 60 reference-prediction pairs from 2 specs, half with only cosmetic changes listed in Appendix E (whitespace, JSON spacing and key order, bullet style) and half with substantive changes (wrong values, missing or extra items, wrong order). Score every pair with string exact match and with a Qwen3-8B judge using the Appendix E system and user templates, then compare acceptance rates on cosmetic versus substantive sets.

follow_ups.title: Scaffold prompt and LoRA adapter ablation
follow_ups.question: How much of the accuracy gain comes from the run-time scaffold prompt versus the trained LoRA weights?
follow_ups.method: For 2 specs, synthesize about 300 training pairs with Qwen3-8B and train Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters. Compare three run-time conditions on held-out tests: frozen base plus scaffold prompt, LoRA plus generic placeholder prompt, and LoRA plus scaffold prompt, using rule-based and Qwen3-8B LEM scoring.

follow_ups.title: LoRA rank and training steps ablation
follow_ups.question: Do larger adapter rank and longer optimization improve correctness within the paper's minute-scale budget?
follow_ups.method: Using about 300 Qwen3-8B-synthesized pairs for one spec, train Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters with rank 8 versus rank 64 (alpha 16) for about 20 versus 80 steps with cosine decay. Compare held-out rule-based and LEM accuracy and final training loss across the four configurations.

follow_ups.title: Teacher example noise and validation filtering
follow_ups.question: What fraction of teacher-synthesized examples violate a rule-checkable spec, and does filtering invalid examples improve the compiled function?
follow_ups.method: For the paper's arXiv /pdf/ extraction spec that must ignore /abs/ links, synthesize about 300 examples with Qwen3-8B using the Appendix D prompt and check each pair with regex ground truth for correct IDs. Train Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters on unfiltered versus filtered sets and compare accuracy on held-out rule-scored inputs containing mixed /pdf/ and /abs/ links.

follow_ups.title: Composed classifier plus answerer pipeline
follow_ups.question: Can two independently compiled functions composed with deterministic branching outperform a single compiled function on a two-step helpdesk task?
follow_ups.method: Define a toy helpdesk task mirroring paw-helper: classify link-versus-answer then produce a cited answer from provided page context. Compile separate Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters for classifier and answerer with about 200 Qwen3-8B pairs each and compose them with Python if-else logic, versus one LoRA trained on about 400 pairs to do both steps, and compare end-to-end accuracy on 50 held-out queries.

follow_ups.title: Valid structured action-program generation
follow_ups.question: Does finetuning improve the rate of syntactically valid and semantically correct action DSL programs compared to prompting?
follow_ups.method: Define a tiny action DSL with allowed verbs, sequence, and repeat counts as in Avatar Director, and synthesize about 300 instruction-to-program pairs with Qwen3-8B. Train a Qwen3-0.6B LoRA and compare it to frozen Qwen3-0.6B prompting on 40 templated unseen instructions, scoring parser validity and verb and structure correctness with deterministic checks.

follow_ups.title: Bidirectional marked-style translation
follow_ups.question: Can separately finetuned adapters add and remove distinctive style markers while preserving meaning as in the English-Claudish demo?
follow_ups.method: Write two specs from Section 6.3: plain-to-marked requiring gate and boundary metaphors and X-shaped and X-gated hyphenations, and marked-to-plain requiring direct English without those devices. Synthesize about 250 pairs per direction with Qwen3-8B, train one Qwen3-0.6B LoRA per direction, and compare to prompted baselines on held-out sentences for meaning preservation (Qwen3-8B judge) and marker presence or absence (regex counts).

follow_ups.title: Check whether Flash-Verify reproduces sequential conditionals
follow_ups.question: Does the two-view verifier actually compute the full-recomputation conditional claimed in Appendix C?
follow_ups.method: Using the linked implementation and BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B, collect up to 16 states with at least four search positions from eight seed-0 GSM8K prompts, with a 128-token generation cap, epsilon=0.9, beta_m=16, and inter-step cache reuse disabled. At the first four search positions, compare the two-view distribution with ordinary full-sequence forwards that commit exactly the confident tokens and preceding drafts; additionally perturb only current and later drafts, which Equation 4 excludes from the conditioning information. Report total variation, argmax disagreements, and confidence changes, rechecking the two largest discrepancies with a float32 PyTorch reference before attributing them to masking semantics.

follow_ups.title: Test whether stale caches encourage self-confirmation
follow_ups.question: How often does cached verification accept a draft that the same verifier rejects after refreshing its context?
follow_ups.method: Run BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B with Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify on 16 seed-0 GSM8K prompts, capped at 128 generated tokens, using epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64, and examine nonterminal states after steps 4 and 12. Clone each state and compare native verification with verification after rebuilding the entire cache from the current draft-state sequence, holding candidate tokens, confident positions, verification order, and attention mask fixed. Measure acceptance reversals, accepted-prefix length, distributional differences, and refresh cost, with prompt-clustered uncertainty intervals and cache-age stratification; treat disagreements as reference sensitivity rather than ground-truth token errors.

follow_ups.title: Compare attention-based refresh-selection signals
follow_ups.question: Does ranking decoded tokens by raw attention logits preserve predictions better than normalized attention, recency, or random refreshes?
follow_ups.method: Using BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B and confidence-aware Flash-Cache without verification, collect two intermediate states from each of 16 seed-0 GSM8K prompts capped at 128 tokens, with epsilon=0.9, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64. From identical cloned caches, compare Equation 2's raw-logit ranking, the corresponding softmax-attention ranking, most-recently-decoded positions, and seeded uniform selection, reserving budget slots for newly decoded tokens in every arm. Compare the next masked-window distributions against a full-recomputation reference using total variation and argmax disagreement, time score construction and refresh separately, and bootstrap over prompts rather than individual tokens.

follow_ups.title: Ablate the verification order
follow_ups.question: Is descending draft confidence the best order for prefix-based acceptance, or can physical token order provide a better accuracy–latency trade-off?
follow_ups.method: Run the linked Flash-dLLM implementation with BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B on 64 seed-0 GSM8K test problems using the paper's 5-shot template, batch size 8, a 256-token cap, epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64. Compare confidence-descending, original-position, and seeded-random search orders, changing the verification mask accordingly while preserving positional embeddings, directly accepted tokens, prefix rejection semantics, and an identical one-token progress fallback. Report exact-match accuracy, accepted-prefix length, rejection reasons, and inference wall time with paired prompt-bootstrap intervals.

follow_ups.title: Intervene on confidence scale without adding information
follow_ups.question: How sensitive are Flash-Verify's acceptance rate and task accuracy to confidence scaling alone?
follow_ups.method: Run BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B with the released Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify on 64 seed-0 GSM8K test problems using 5-shot prompts, batch size 8, a 256-token cap, epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64. Compare temperatures T=0.7, 1.0, and 1.3 applied only to verifier logits when computing threshold probabilities, leaving candidate argmaxes and draft ordering unchanged within each step and using the same progress fallback. Measure threshold-pass rates, accepted tokens per pass, exact-match accuracy, and inference time with paired intervals, distinguishing mechanically increased confidence from improved answer quality.

follow_ups.title: Replace per-token thresholds with a cumulative confidence budget
follow_ups.question: Can a cumulative verifier-confidence budget improve the accuracy–latency trade-off relative to a fixed gamma?
follow_ups.method: Use BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B and the linked implementation on 64 seed-0 GSM8K test problems with 5-shot prompts, batch size 8, a 256-token cap, epsilon=0.9, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64. Compare fixed gamma values of 0.8 and 0.9 with accepting the longest agreeing prefix whose product of mask-view probabilities remains at least 1-delta, for delta=0.4 and 0.6, leaving directly accepted tokens unchanged and using the same one-token fallback. Report all four accuracy–latency operating points, prefix lengths, probability products, and fallback counts with paired uncertainty intervals, treating the product as a verifier-based score rather than a demonstrated task-correctness guarantee.

follow_ups.title: Invoke verification only when its estimated benefit exceeds its cost
follow_ups.question: Can a lightweight online controller avoid unproductive verification, especially at batch size one?
follow_ups.method: Using the linked implementation and BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B, compare always verifying, never verifying, and cost-gated verification on 32 seed-0 GSM8K test problems at batch sizes 1 and 8, with 5-shot prompts, a 256-token cap, epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64. The batch-level controller verifies when extra accepted tokens per verification-second estimated from its last four probes exceeds the current draft's directly accepted tokens per draft-second, with mandatory probes on the first and every fourth step and a common progress fallback. Include controller and timing overhead in inference wall time, and report accuracy, verification frequency, accepted tokens per model pass, and paired latency differences.

follow_ups.title: Isolate the benefit of kernel fusion
follow_ups.question: How much A100 latency and memory improvement comes from fusion itself, rather than cache layout, token selection, or decoding changes?
follow_ups.method: Reuse the released Flash-Cache kernel and one middle layer of BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B, comparing fused projection/RoPE/cache writing with an unfused PyTorch reference using identical weights, query indices, preallocated flat caches, and the same subsequent attention kernel. Benchmark batch sizes 1 and 8, cache lengths 512 and 2048, and query lengths 64 and 144, with deterministic inputs, 20 warmups, and 100 CUDA-event repetitions per configuration in randomized arm order. Report numerical discrepancies, update-path and update-plus-attention latency, peak allocated memory, and kernel counts from a separate profiler trace, rather than attributing end-to-end decoding gains to fusion.

follow_ups.title: Measure scheduling gains under controlled batch heterogeneity
follow_ups.question: Does scheduled attention improve efficiency specifically when requests need different amounts of recomputation?
follow_ups.method: Using the released scheduled-attention kernel and LLaDA-1.5-8B attention dimensions, construct deterministic BF16 GPU queries against 1024-position caches at batch sizes 8 and 16, with workloads containing all 64-token queries, all 1024-token queries, or 25% long and 75% short queries. Compare block-table packing, padding to the longest query, and separate length-bucket dispatch while keeping the attention kernel, cache layout, and valid queries identical. After 20 warmups, measure 100 repetitions of latency, useful query rows per second, and peak memory, checking equality of valid outputs and reporting correctness failures separately from speed results.

follow_ups.title: Evaluate code-generation goodput under an explicit quality constraint
follow_ups.question: Do Flash-Verify's throughput gains persist when counting correct programs and requiring a bounded accuracy loss?
follow_ups.method: With BF16 LLaDA-1.5-8B and the linked implementation, use 16 calibration and 128 disjoint evaluation MBPP problems sampled with seed 0, the paper's 3-shot prompting and post-processing, batch size 8, a 256-token cap, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64 to compare confidence-only decoding at epsilon=0.9 with verification at gamma=0.8, 0.85, or 0.9. Freeze the fastest gamma whose calibration pass@1 is no lower than the baseline's before evaluation; if none qualifies, report that failure and evaluate gamma=0.9 only as a diagnostic. Run public unit tests in CPU-time-limited subprocesses, and report held-out pass@1, useful tokens before EOS per inference-second, correct programs per inference-second, and paired confidence intervals, claiming noninferiority only if the accuracy-difference interval excludes losses exceeding a preregistered three-percentage-point margin.

follow_ups.title: Acceptance-rule ablation: draft/mask agreement test vs. mask-view confidence gate
follow_ups.question: Which component of Flash-Verify's acceptance rule (the draft/mask-view agreement test, or the mask-view confidence threshold gamma) is responsible for preserving accuracy, and what does each component cost or gain in tokens decoded per step?
follow_ups.method: Using the authors' Flash-dLLM code with LLaDA-1.5 (paper defaults: Flash-Cache, beta_t=64, beta_m=64, epsilon=0.9, 5-shot GSM8K, generation length 256, batch 32) on 128 GSM8K test problems, run four decoders: (a) full rule (accept if draft and mask-view tokens agree and c~>=0.8, stop at first failure), (b) agreement-only (gamma=0), (c) threshold-only (commit the mask-view token x~ whenever c~>=0.8 with no agreement check, stopping at the first c~<0.8), and (d) confidence-aware decoding without verification. Report accuracy, tokens per step, tokens per forward pass, verify-pass acceptance rate and throughput; treat the per-step statistics (aggregated over thousands of steps) as the primary readout, since accuracy differences below ~3 points are within sampling noise at this size and a null accuracy difference does not establish equivalence.

follow_ups.title: Cost and value of the stop-at-first-mismatch prefix rule
follow_ups.question: How many search tokens that individually pass the agree-and-gamma test are discarded by the first-mismatch prefix rule, and does accepting them (so later verify conditionals include rejected drafts in their context) change tokens per step or accuracy?
follow_ups.method: Run default Flash-Verify (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, gamma=0.8, epsilon=0.9, beta_t=beta_m=64, length 256, 5-shot GSM8K) on 160 GSM8K problems twice: with the paper's prefix rule, and with non-prefix acceptance where every search token satisfying agree AND c~>=gamma is committed regardless of earlier mismatches in causality order. Log per verify pass the number of tokens that pass the local test but are discarded by the prefix rule, and report tokens per step, throughput, accuracy, and the final-answer agreement rate between the two variants.

follow_ups.title: Does the causality order matter? Confidence-descending vs. left-to-right vs. random
follow_ups.question: Is sorting search tokens by draft confidence the best order for the chain-rule verify pass, or do positional (left-to-right) or random orders yield longer accepted prefixes, more tokens per step, or better accuracy?
follow_ups.method: Keep default Flash-Verify (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, gamma=0.8, epsilon=0.9, beta_t=beta_m=64, length 256, 5-shot) and change only the order in which search tokens are arranged for the causal verify mask and prefix acceptance: draft-confidence descending (paper), left-to-right by position, and uniformly random with a fixed seed. On 128 GSM8K problems report mean accepted-prefix length per verify pass, tokens per step, throughput, and accuracy for each ordering.

follow_ups.title: Direct acceptance vs. verify-everything: sweeping epsilon under Flash-Verify
follow_ups.question: With a verify pass available, is it better to keep accepting high-marginal-confidence tokens directly (epsilon=0.9), to accept more of them directly (epsilon=0.7), or to route every token through the chain-rule verify pass (epsilon=1.0, so the direct-accept set D^t is empty)?
follow_ups.method: Run Flash-Verify (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, gamma=0.8, beta_t=beta_m=64, length 256, 5-shot) on 128 GSM8K problems with epsilon in {0.7, 0.9, 1.0}, plus confidence-aware decoding at epsilon=0.9 as an in-session control. Report accuracy, tokens per step, tokens per forward pass, the share of committed tokens that came from the verify pass versus direct acceptance, and throughput.

follow_ups.title: Fidelity to one-token-per-step sequential decoding
follow_ups.question: Are Flash-Verify outputs closer to the sequential greedy decoder (the model's own sequential distribution that Theorem 1 bounds deviation against) than confidence-aware outputs are, and does the tokens-per-step gain concentrate on problems the greedy decoder solves?
follow_ups.method: On 96 GSM8K problems (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, length 256, 5-shot, deterministic argmax), run the repo's greedy one-token-per-step decoder, confidence-aware decoding at epsilon=0.9, and Flash-Verify at gamma=0.8. For each parallel decoder report the exact-match rate of the full generation with the greedy output, token-level normalized edit distance to it, final-answer agreement with greedy, and accuracy; additionally report tokens per step separately for problems the greedy decoder answered correctly versus incorrectly.

follow_ups.title: Is the verify pass worth running every step? Zero-acceptance predictability and a skip rule
follow_ups.question: What fraction of verify passes accept no tokens, can that be predicted from the draft pass alone (maximum draft confidence in the search set), and does skipping predicted-useless passes raise tokens per forward pass without hurting accuracy?
follow_ups.method: Instrument default Flash-Verify (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, gamma=0.8, epsilon=0.9, beta_t=beta_m=64, length 256, 5-shot) on 160 GSM8K problems to log per step |S^t|, the maximum draft confidence in S^t, the number of verify-accepted tokens, and (c, c~, agree) for every search token; report the zero-acceptance fraction, the AUC of max draft confidence for predicting at least one acceptance, and mean c~ minus c for accepted versus rejected tokens. Then choose from the logs the threshold tau that would skip about 30% of verify passes while losing the fewest acceptances, rerun with the rule 'run the verify pass only if max draft confidence in S^t >= tau' (committing the single top draft token on steps that would otherwise commit nothing), and compare tokens per forward pass, throughput, and accuracy with the unskipped run.

follow_ups.title: Diagnosing the code-generation accuracy drop: does a stricter gamma recover HumanEval pass@1?
follow_ups.question: Is Flash-Verify's HumanEval accuracy loss relative to confidence-aware decoding (Table 1) a gamma-calibration problem that a stricter gamma fixes while retaining a tokens-per-step advantage, or does the loss persist at high gamma?
follow_ups.method: On the first 120 HumanEval problems (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, 0-shot, length 256, beta_t=beta_m=64, epsilon=0.9), run confidence-aware decoding and Flash-Verify with gamma in {0.85, 0.95, 0.99}, scoring pass@1 by executing generations with the human-eval harness (with timeouts) after stop-sequence truncation and code-block extraction. Report pass@1, tokens per step, throughput, and mean accepted-prefix length for each gamma, noting that pass@1 differences below about 5 points are within noise at n=120.

follow_ups.title: Transfer to a different checkpoint: LLaDA-8B-Instruct
follow_ups.question: Does Flash-Verify's roughly 2x tokens-per-step gain over confidence-aware decoding at comparable accuracy hold on LLaDA-8B-Instruct (the checkpoint LLaDA-1.5 was derived from), or does it depend on LLaDA-1.5's particular confidence profile?
follow_ups.method: Run the Flash-dLLM code unchanged with GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct (download only this model) on 160 GSM8K problems (5-shot, length 256, batch 16, Flash-Cache, beta_t=beta_m=64) under confidence-aware decoding at epsilon=0.9 and Flash-Verify at gamma=0.8. Report accuracy, tokens per step, throughput, mean draft confidence and verify acceptance rate, and compare the Flash-Verify/confidence-aware ratios with the LLaDA-1.5 values reported in Table 5a (5.6 vs 2.8 tokens/step, 198.4 vs 140.4 tokens/s at length 256, batch 16).

follow_ups.title: Open-ended generation: does the verify advantage shrink when confidence is flatter?
follow_ups.question: On open-ended instruction prompts, the regime the authors list as untested, does Flash-Verify's tokens-per-step and acceptance advantage over confidence-aware decoding shrink relative to GSM8K, and do its outputs degenerate?
follow_ups.method: Use 96 open-ended prompts from a public instruction dataset (e.g., Dolly-15k creative-writing and open-QA categories) and 96 GSM8K prompts as an in-session control, each decoded with confidence-aware decoding at epsilon=0.9 and Flash-Verify at gamma=0.8 (LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, beta_t=beta_m=64, length 256, instruct chat template). Report tokens per step, verify-pass acceptance rate, mean draft and mask-view confidence, output length to EOS, and degeneration proxies (distinct-3 and repeated-4-gram rate), comparing the Flash-Verify/confidence-aware ratios between the two prompt sets.

follow_ups.title: Selective cache update: attention-based tracking vs. recency vs. random at equal budget
follow_ups.question: Does choosing tracked tokens by the attention they receive from masked queries (top-k of a_i) matter for accuracy and speed, compared with tracking the most recently decoded tokens or a random subset at the same budget beta_t?
follow_ups.method: In the Flash-dLLM code, replace the top-k attention-score selection of the tracking set with (a) the beta_t minus |D^t| most recently decoded tokens and (b) a uniformly random subset of decoded tokens with a fixed seed, always including the newly decoded tokens D^t; run default Flash-Verify (LLaDA-1.5, gamma=0.8, epsilon=0.9, beta_t=beta_m=64, length 256, 5-shot) on 128 GSM8K problems with the three criteria. Report accuracy, tokens per step, throughput, and final-answer agreement with the attention-based run; if time permits, add beta_t=16 with attention-based selection as a low-budget reference point.

follow_ups.title: Does Flash-Verify's single verify pass compute the exact sequential conditional its guarantee assumes?
follow_ups.question: Appendix C (Assumption 1, Remark 1) treats the mask-view output at search rank k as exactly the model's sequential conditional given the committed drafts of ranks 1..k−1. In the shared pass, however, the context cannot attend to drafts, and drafts reuse the mask views' position ids. How close are the two distributions in practice, and how often does the gap flip accept/reject decisions?
follow_ups.method: Implement no-cache Flash-Verify for LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5, bf16) with explicit position ids and a boolean attention mask: draft copies of the search positions are appended with duplicated position ids; ranks follow descending draft confidence; the mask view at rank k sees all non-search positions, drafts of ranks 1..k−1 and mask views of ranks k..K; the draft at rank k sees non-search positions, drafts 1..k and mask views k+1..K; non-search positions see each other and all mask views but no drafts. Decode GSM8K test problems (0-shot chat-template prompt, generation length 256, window = leftmost 64 still-masked positions, ε=0.9, γ=0.8, at least one token per step; ~100 problems or 20 minutes, whichever comes first), and at every 4th step compute the exact conditional for the first 8 search ranks with a separate full bidirectional forward in which D^t and the drafts of ranks 1..k−1 are filled in and everything else stays masked. Report by rank the total-variation distance and argmax agreement between single-pass and exact distributions (with draft-marginal-versus-exact as a baseline), how often the γ=0.8 accept/reject decision differs, and the accepted-prefix length under single-pass versus exact conditionals, with bootstrap CIs over problems.

follow_ups.title: Token-level deviation from slow greedy decoding: Flash-Verify versus cheaper commit rules at equal forward-pass cost
follow_ups.question: Remark 2 argues that verifying is not equivalent to lowering ε. Per forward pass spent, does Flash-Verify commit tokens that agree with one-token-per-pass greedy decoding more often than lower-ε thresholding or entropy-bounded unmasking? Which parts of the verify rule are responsible: the agreement test, the γ gate, prefix stopping, or the causality order (the paper describes both confidence-ordered and left-to-right)?
follow_ups.method: From LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5) no-cache confidence-aware trajectories (ε=0.9, 0-shot GSM8K, generation length 256, window = leftmost 64 still-masked positions), take ~300 states (every 6th step of ~50 problems, within 20 minutes); at each state run one draft pass, two Flash-Verify verify passes (search ranks by descending draft confidence or left-to-right; draft copies with duplicated position ids under the Appendix C mask), and a reference that fills the whole window by one-token-per-pass greedy decoding (most confident masked position first). Offline, apply to every state: ε-thresholding (ε from 0.95 down to 0.5); entropy-bounded unmasking (commit lowest-entropy window positions while cumulative entropy ≤ η, η∈{0.1,0.3,1,3}); and Flash-Verify (ε=0.9, γ∈{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}) in both orders plus agreement-only, γ-only (commit the mask-view argmax, stopping after the first disagreement with the draft) and no-prefix variants, each rule committing at least one token. Plot each rule's fraction of committed tokens that differ from the reference against tokens committed per forward pass (verify rules cost two passes), compare rules at matched tokens per pass with bootstrap CIs over problems, and break deviations down by token type (digits vs other) and by confidence bin to test whether mask-view confidence is better calibrated than draft confidence.

follow_ups.title: GSM8K accuracy of Flash-Verify versus cheaper single-pass parallel decoders at matched forward passes
follow_ups.question: Fig. 6 compares decoders per iteration, but a Flash-Verify iteration costs two forward passes (Table 6: 5.7 tokens per two-pass step versus 2.8 per one-pass step for confidence-aware decoding). At matched forward passes per generated token, is Flash-Verify more accurate than confidence-aware decoding with a lower ε or than entropy-bounded unmasking?
follow_ups.method: Use LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5) with no KV cache (so only the commit rule differs), 0-shot chat-template GSM8K prompts, generation length 256 and a window of the leftmost 64 still-masked positions. Run five arms on the same test problems: confidence-aware ε=0.9 and ε=0.7; entropy-bounded unmasking (commit lowest-entropy window positions while cumulative entropy ≤ η) with η=0.3 and η=1.0; and Flash-Verify (ε=0.9, γ=0.8, verify pass per Appendix C with duplicated position ids). Every arm commits at least one token per step, and all arms are cycled per problem until ~20 minutes of decoding elapse (target ≥120 problems). Report per arm the accuracy (last number vs gold), forward passes per content token (tokens before the first EOS, verify passes included), and the error rate of regex-extracted arithmetic statements ('a op b = c', including <<…>> annotations) as a more sensitive quality signal; compare Flash-Verify with the single-pass arm(s) nearest in passes per token using paired bootstrap CIs and McNemar tests, reading CIs that span zero as inconclusive rather than as equivalence.

follow_ups.title: Ablating the tracked-set selection rule in Flash-Cache's selective cache update
follow_ups.question: Fig. 1b motivates choosing tracked tokens by attention, but the selection criterion is never ablated. At a fixed budget β_t, does Eq. 2 (accumulated pre-softmax logits) give more faithful window predictions and higher accuracy than softmax attention mass, recency, random choice, or tracking only newly decoded tokens?
follow_ups.method: Implement the paper's cached decoding for LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5) in PyTorch. One full forward fills per-layer K/V buffers for all positions; after that, each step recomputes only the 64-position masked window (leftmost still-masked positions) plus β_t=64 tracked positions (newly decoded tokens plus β_t−|D^t| chosen from earlier decoded positions, prompt included) with explicit position ids, attends bidirectionally over the whole buffer, and overwrites those positions' entries; decode with confidence-aware commits (ε=0.9, ≥1 token per step) on 0-shot GSM8K at generation length 256. Run six arms on the same problems: tracked tokens chosen by Eq. 2 logits, by mean softmax attention mass from window queries, by recency, at random (fixed seed), newly-decoded-only, and an exact no-cache reference; cycle arms per problem until ~20 minutes of decoding elapse (target ≥120 problems), and at every 5th step also run an exact full forward on the current sequence. Report the total-variation distance and argmax agreement of window predictions between cached and exact passes (overall and by decoding progress), accuracy (last number vs gold), and answer agreement with the no-cache arm, with paired bootstrap CIs over problems.

follow_ups.title: Do the most-attended decoded tokens have the most stale keys and values?
follow_ups.question: Selective cache update refreshes the decoded tokens that window queries attend to most. Are these the positions whose keys and values actually drift across denoising steps, or are they mostly stable attention-sink tokens (chat template, punctuation, newline) whose refresh changes little?

follow_ups.title: Where Flash-dLLM's speed comes from on an A100: IO fusion versus query size, batching and tokens per step
follow_ups.question: The 1.37× Flash-Cache gain comes from an RTX 3090 per-layer breakdown (Fig. 1a) whose components are linear projection, positional embedding, position gather and attention. On an A100 at the paper's step shapes, what share of a full decoding step (including MLP and LM head) do the fused operations take? How much full-step speedup does fusion give, and how much of the reported throughputs remains unexplained once query-set size, batch size and tokens per step are accounted for?

follow_ups.title: Does Flash-Verify cost accuracy on code generation, and through which failure modes?
follow_ups.question: Table 1 reports no-cache Flash-Verify at 37.20% on HumanEval at both lengths, versus 42.68% (length 256) and 39.63% (length 512) for no-cache confidence-aware decoding. Does a paired re-test reproduce a loss on code, and is any loss driven by syntax or indentation breakage from parallel commits or by logic errors?
follow_ups.method: Decode the 164 HumanEval problems with LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5; 0-shot chat-template prompt asking for the completed function in a code block, generation length 256, window = leftmost 64 still-masked positions, no KV cache, ≥1 token per step) under two arms, cycling both per problem (stop at 22 minutes if needed): confidence-aware decoding (ε=0.9) and Flash-Verify (ε=0.9, γ=0.85 as in Table 3, verify pass per Appendix C with duplicated position ids). Extract the code and run it against the unit tests in a subprocess with a 10 s timeout. Report pass@1 per arm, the paired difference with McNemar's exact test and a bootstrap CI, tokens per step and forward passes per content token, and per-arm failure counts by type (fails ast.parse, runtime exception, assertion failure, timeout), treating a CI that spans zero as inconclusive.

follow_ups.title: Flash-Verify on open-ended prompts with flatter confidence distributions
follow_ups.question: The paper's limitations flag open-ended generation, where token confidences are flatter, as untested. On such prompts, does Flash-Verify still commit substantially more tokens per forward pass than confidence-aware decoding, and does output quality change?
follow_ups.method: Take 80 prompts from databricks-dolly-15k (creative_writing, brainstorming, open_qa, general_qa) plus 40 GSM8K problems as a structured contrast, and generate 256 tokens with LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5; no cache, window = leftmost 64 still-masked positions, ≥1 token per step) using two arms: confidence-aware decoding (ε=0.9) and Flash-Verify (ε=0.9, γ=0.8, verify pass per Appendix C). Log per step how many tokens were committed via ε versus via verification, and the window's mean draft confidence. Report tokens per step and per forward pass by prompt type, repetition metrics (distinct-2, fraction of repeated 4-grams), and, for the Dolly pairs, a preference judged by Qwen3-8B (thinking disabled) in both presentation orders with ties allowed, with bootstrap CIs over prompts.

follow_ups.title: Does the stale tracked cache change Flash-Verify's decisions?
follow_ups.question: Appendix C's guarantee is stated for exact model conditionals, but the headline Flash-Cache + Flash-Verify configuration runs both passes against a cache that is refreshed only at tracked positions. How far do cached draft and mask-view distributions drift from exact recomputation, and how often does this change which tokens are committed?

follow_ups.title: Sliding-window versus block decoding schedule as a possible confound in Table 1's accuracy comparisons
follow_ups.question: Flash-Cache, an approximation, scores above exact no-cache decoding in 14 of 16 Table 1 cells (by up to 3.8 points), and no-cache Flash-Verify beats no-cache confidence decoding on math. How much accuracy difference does the candidate-set schedule alone produce under identical exact decoding: a sliding window over the leftmost 64 masked positions versus fixed semi-autoregressive blocks?
follow_ups.method: With LLaDA-1.5 (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5) and no KV cache, run confidence-aware decoding (ε=0.9, ≥1 token per step, generation length 256, 0-shot GSM8K) on the same problems under three candidate-set schedules: a sliding window over the leftmost 64 still-masked positions (as in Flash-Cache), fixed semi-autoregressive blocks of 32 tokens, and fixed blocks of 64 tokens; cycle all arms per problem until ~20 minutes of decoding elapse (target ≥170 problems). Report accuracy (last number vs gold), tokens per step and the rate of missing or truncated answers per arm, with paired bootstrap CIs and McNemar tests for each pairwise difference. A schedule gap comparable to Table 1's cache-vs-no-cache gaps would indicate that those comparisons could be confounded by schedule; CIs spanning zero are inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect.

follow_ups.title: Check verification against sequential recomputation
follow_ups.question: Does the two-view verifier reproduce the sequential conditionals assumed in Appendix C, including when cached states are refreshed?
follow_ups.method: Using the paper’s Flash-dLLM repository and GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B), capture 16 active decoding states from one-shot GSM8K test prompts with generation length 128, tracking budget 64, masked window 16, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8. Freeze drafts and confidence order, then compare distributions at up to eight search positions from cached verification, fully refreshed verification, and separate full bidirectional recomputation with the confident set and exactly the preceding draft prefix committed. Report total variation, argmax disagreement, and confidence differences; additionally perturb only later drafts, restoring the starting cache each time, to test whether earlier mask-view predictions leak information from them.

follow_ups.title: Isolate the benefit of KV-cache kernel fusion
follow_ups.question: How much latency and memory improvement comes from fusion itself rather than a different cache policy or query workload?
follow_ups.method: Load GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B) through the paper’s repository and benchmark one representative transformer layer at batch sizes 1 and 8, per-request query lengths 32, 64, and 128, and cache lengths 512 and 2048. Compare the released fused projection/RoPE/cache-write path with separate PyTorch operations using identical weights, inputs, positions, and downstream attention, checking Q/K/V and attention-output numerical errors before interpreting speedups. Use 20 warm-up and 100 timed repetitions per configuration, reporting synchronized CUDA-event latency, incremental peak allocation, and kernel counts from a brief profiler trace, with compilation time reported separately.

follow_ups.title: Measure scheduling gains on controlled ragged batches
follow_ups.question: Does block-table scheduling materially help when query lengths diverge, independently of cache approximation and decoding decisions?
follow_ups.method: Using the released Flash-dLLM attention kernel and GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B), benchmark one attention layer with batch size 16 and cache length 2048: compare uniform queries of length 128 with a ragged batch containing two lengths of 512, eight of 32, and six of 128, giving equal total valid queries. Compare packed block-table execution with the same kernel processing queries padded to the batch maximum, keeping KV tensors read-only and discarding padded outputs. Verify valid-output agreement and report warmed latency distributions, incremental peak memory, and numbers of useful versus padded blocks over 100 repetitions.

follow_ups.title: Attention tracking versus recency and random tracking
follow_ups.question: At a fixed refresh budget, does attention-based tracking preserve predictions and task accuracy better than simpler token-selection policies?
follow_ups.method: Run GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B) with the paper’s repository on the first 32 one-shot GSM8K test questions, generation length 256, batch size 8, tracking budget 64, masked window 32, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8. Compare Equation 2 tracking, most-recent-token tracking, and uniform random tracking with three fixed random seeds, always reserving identical mandatory slots for newly decoded tokens; at the first steps after 64 and 128 output tokens are committed, compare cached draft predictions with full recomputation without altering generation. Report exact-match accuracy, prediction divergence, denoising steps, selection overhead, and total latency with question-paired bootstrap intervals, treating recomputation agreement as model consistency rather than semantic correctness.

follow_ups.title: Raw attention logits versus normalized attention weights
follow_ups.question: Does Equation 2’s unnormalized-logit ranking identify the states most worth refreshing, or does normalized attention mass work better?
follow_ups.method: Using the paper’s repository and GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B), generate 256-token continuations for 16 one-shot GSM8K test prompts with tracking budget 64, masked window 32, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8, collecting up to 24 states after at least 96 output positions are decoded. At each cloned state, refresh the same newly decoded positions and fill the remaining tracking slots using either Equation 2 or attention probabilities normalized over all keys and aggregated over the same heads and layers, then predict the unchanged next masked window. Report ranking overlap, normalized attention mass captured, distribution divergence from full recomputation, argmax disagreement, and scoring overhead, with uncertainty clustered by prompt.

follow_ups.title: Quantify stale-cache effects on verification acceptance
follow_ups.question: How often do stale KV states change acceptance decisions or increase verifier confidence relative to freshly recomputed states?
follow_ups.method: Run Flash-Verify from the paper’s repository with GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B) on 24 one-shot GSM8K test prompts, generation length 256, batch size 4, tracking budget 64, masked window 32, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8, inspecting active states at iterations 4, 8, 16, and 32. Replay each state with its original cache and with a cache fully refreshed from the current sequence including directly accepted tokens, holding draft IDs, order, tracking selection, verify queries, and attention masks fixed. Measure confidence shifts, total variation, acceptance flips, and accepted-prefix length changes against cache age and decoding progress, using prompt-clustered intervals and explicitly treating fresh verification as a model reference rather than ground truth.

follow_ups.title: A cost-matched mask-only verification ablation
follow_ups.question: Are verification gains attributable to conditioning on earlier draft tokens rather than simply another forward pass or a lower acceptance threshold?
follow_ups.method: Using the released code and GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B), evaluate the first 32 one-shot GSM8K test questions at generation length 256 and batch size 8, with tracking budget 64, masked window 32, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8. Compare standard Flash-Verify with a per-pass cost-matched control that replaces search-position draft-view inputs with MASK while preserving query sizes, masks, directly accepted inputs, and agreement checks against the original draft IDs; also run confidence-only decoding at epsilon values 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9. Report exact-match accuracy with paired intervals, latency, generated-token counts, and total forward-query tokens, comparing accuracy–cost operating points rather than assuming equal threshold values imply equal cost.

follow_ups.title: Confidence order versus positional order
follow_ups.question: Is confidence-sorted causality order important for verification efficiency, and does its effect differ between mathematics and code?
follow_ups.method: With the paper’s repository and GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B), run the first 24 one-shot GSM8K test questions and first 24 three-shot MBPP test problems at generation length 256, batch size 8, tracking budget 64, masked window 32, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8. Compare descending draft confidence, original token position, and a fixed seeded random search order, stopping acceptance at the first failed agreement or confidence gate in every condition. Report accepted-prefix lengths, rejection positions, latency, GSM8K exact match, and MBPP pass@1 using isolated two-second test subprocesses, with paired bootstrap intervals separately for each task.

follow_ups.title: Gold-token calibration of draft and verified confidence
follow_ups.question: Do higher mask-view confidences correspond to more correct predictions, or mainly to more confident self-agreement?
follow_ups.method: Load GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B) through the paper’s repository and construct answer-only infilling probes from 128 one-shot GSM8K test items by masking each canonical gold integer’s token span, revealing its length equally across conditions. With fully refreshed caches, epsilon=0.9, and gamma=0.8, record draft and mask-view verification distributions before prefix rejection, using model drafts—not gold tokens—as verifier context, and label token predictions by canonical gold-token agreement. Report token accuracy, reliability bins, Brier score, calibration error, and threshold precision with question-clustered intervals, separating all candidates from accepted prefixes and identifying this as a length-revealed probe rather than standard GSM8K generation accuracy.

follow_ups.title: Cumulative-confidence acceptance budgets
follow_ups.question: Can budgeting uncertainty across the verified prefix improve the accuracy–latency trade-off over a fixed per-token threshold?
follow_ups.method: Using the paper’s repository and GPU BF16 LLaDA-1.5 (8B), evaluate the first 64 one-shot GSM8K test questions with generation length 256, batch size 8, tracking budget 64, masked window 32, and epsilon=0.9. Compare fixed gamma values 0.8 and 0.9 with acceptance of the longest agreeing prefix whose cumulative product of mask-view confidences remains at least 1−delta, for preregistered delta values 0.2 and 0.5, leaving directly accepted confident tokens unchanged. Report exact-match accuracy, latency, forward-query tokens, accepted-prefix length, and observed cumulative confidence with paired bootstrap intervals, treating the confidence product as an internal model surrogate rather than a guarantee of correct answers.

follow_ups.title: A100 validation of the fused KV-update kernel
follow_ups.question: Does fusing QKV projection, RoPE, and cache writes reduce latency and temporary memory on the A100 used in the paper's main evaluation, without changing the computed states?
follow_ups.method: Using one LLaDA-1.5 transformer layer and its projection weights, compare the Flash-Cache fused QKV-projection/RoPE/cache-write path with the separate operations described in the paper at query lengths 16 and 64 and cache lengths 256 and 512. On the A100, measure maximum K/V error, warmed CUDA-event latency, kernel-launch count, and peak temporary allocation over 100 repetitions per shape.

follow_ups.title: Does attention-based tracking beat simpler token-selection rules?
follow_ups.question: At the same tracking budget, does selecting tokens by attention improve accuracy or speed over selecting recent or random decoded tokens?
follow_ups.method: On LLaDA-1.5, run confidence-aware Flash-Cache on the first 32 GSM8K five-shot evaluation items with generation length 128 and batch size 4, using epsilon=0.9, beta_m=64, and beta_t=64. Change only the tracking rule among attention top-k, most-recent decoded tokens, and seeded random tokens, always including newly decoded tokens, then report exact-match accuracy and tokens/s; repeat the random rule with three fixed seeds.

follow_ups.title: Measure stale-cache logit drift against full recomputation
follow_ups.question: How much does the approximate cache change masked-token predictions, and how does that drift depend on the tracking budget?
follow_ups.method: Run cached, confidence-aware LLaDA-1.5 decoding on 12 fixed GSM8K five-shot prompts with beta_m=64, beta_t in {32, 64, 96}, generation length 64, batch size 1, and no Flash-Verify. At denoising steps 2, 8, and 16, recompute all KV states from that exact current sequence and compare full-forward logits on the masked window with cached-path logits, reporting mean KL divergence and top-1 agreement.

follow_ups.title: Check the verifier mask against sequential conditionals
follow_ups.question: Does Flash-Verify's two-view mask reproduce the model's sequential conditional at the positions it verifies?
follow_ups.method: Run Flash-Verify without KV caching on eight fixed GSM8K prompts with generation length 64, saving drafts and contexts at the first two verify steps and examining the first four search positions in causal order. For each position, compare the two-view mask-view logits with a separate full-sequence forward conditioned on the same prompt, decoded context, confident tokens, and earlier search drafts, while the current and later search positions remain [MASK]; report KL divergence and top-1 agreement.

follow_ups.title: Adaptive versus fixed Flash-Verify threshold
follow_ups.question: Can a simple online gamma controller improve the speed-accuracy trade-off over fixed verification thresholds?
follow_ups.method: On the first 32 GSM8K five-shot items, run LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify at epsilon=0.9, beta_t=64, beta_m=64, batch size 4, and generation length 128. Compare fixed gamma values 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 with a controller starting at 0.8 that every four verify steps raises gamma by 0.05 if the mean accepted search tokens per step exceeds five and lowers it by 0.05 otherwise, clipped to [0.6, 1.0]; report exact-match accuracy, accepted tokens per step, and tokens/s.

follow_ups.title: Do verify thresholds transfer across tasks?
follow_ups.question: Can one fixed verify threshold serve both mathematical reasoning and code generation, or are task-specific thresholds useful?
follow_ups.method: Use LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify on the first 24 GSM8K five-shot items and first 24 HumanEval zero-shot tasks, at generation length 128, batch size 4, epsilon=0.9, beta_t=64, and beta_m=64. Run gamma=0.8 and gamma=0.85 on both tasks, then report flexible_extract accuracy or pass@1, tokens/s, and per-example bootstrap intervals, treating this small-subset comparison as exploratory rather than as evidence of equivalence.

follow_ups.title: Paired quality audit of confidence-aware and Flash-Verify decoding
follow_ups.question: On the same problems, how often does Flash-Verify change correctness relative to confidence-aware decoding, and how uncertain is the accuracy difference?
follow_ups.method: Run confidence-aware Flash-Cache and Flash-Cache with Flash-Verify on the same first 24 GSM8K five-shot and 24 MATH four-shot items using LLaDA-1.5, batch size 4, generation length 128, beta_m=64, beta_t=64, epsilon=0.9, two fixed seeds, and gamma=0.8 for GSM8K and 0.85 for MATH. Score with flexible_extract and math_verify, tabulate paired correct-to-wrong and wrong-to-correct transitions, and compute a problem-level paired bootstrap interval for the accuracy difference alongside throughput.

follow_ups.title: Scheduled attention with heterogeneous query lengths
follow_ups.question: Does the block-table scheduler reduce latency and padding waste when query lengths within a batch differ?
follow_ups.method: Using LLaDA-1.5 head dimensions on the A100, construct fixed random Q/K/V blocks for eight sequences with query lengths 16, 16, 32, 32, 64, 64, 96, and 96 and common KV length 512; compare the paper's block-table scheduled attention with conventional padding to length 96, plus an equal-length control. Check output error, padded query slots, and warmed latency over 100 repetitions.

follow_ups.title: Memory scaling of flat versus conventional KV-cache layouts
follow_ups.question: Does the flat preallocated cache retain a memory advantage over a conventional four-dimensional KV cache as batch size and generation length grow?
follow_ups.method: On LLaDA-1.5, use the first 16 GSM8K one-shot items and greedy KV decoding to compare the flat preallocated Flash-Cache layout with a conventional four-dimensional KV-cache implementation at batch sizes 1, 8, and 16 and generation lengths 128 and 256, keeping dtype and query schedule fixed. Record peak CUDA memory and tokens/s for each configuration, and check output agreement.

follow_ups.title: Cross-model test on Dream-Coder-7B
follow_ups.question: Do Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify work on a second masked diffusion model discussed in the paper, beyond LLaDA-1.5?
follow_ups.method: Load the open Dream-Coder-7B diffusion model named in the paper on the A100 and run the first 16 MBPP three-shot items at generation length 128 and batch size 2. Compare no-cache confidence-aware decoding, Flash-Cache confidence-aware decoding, and Flash-Cache with Flash-Verify using epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, beta_m=64, and beta_t=48; report pass@1, tokens/s, peak memory, and whether the cache kernel runs without model-specific changes.

follow_ups.title: Per-layer KV-cache IO breakdown on A100
follow_ups.question: Does the fused Flash-Cache kernel remove the RoPE and cache-write HBM bottleneck and give the ~1.37x per-layer speedup claimed in Fig 1a?
follow_ups.method: Clone https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM and run LLaDA-1.5 on 10 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 128 and batch size 1, timing only the first 10 denoising steps. Time per-layer QKV projection, RoPE plus gather-positions, cache write, and attention separately for the conventional PyTorch cache path versus the fused Triton Flash-Cache kernel and compare total latency.

follow_ups.title: Top-k attention mass across layers
follow_ups.question: Do the top-32 most-attended decoded tokens capture ~50% of attention weight in middle layers as in Fig 1b?
follow_ups.method: Clone Flash-dLLM repo and run LLaDA-1.5 without KV caching on 20 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 128, dumping per-layer attention logits from masked queries to decoded tokens for the first 20 steps. For each layer compute the share of total decoded-token attention mass held by the top-32 most-attended decoded tokens averaged over steps and examples.

follow_ups.title: Confidence versus early-decodable count correlation
follow_ups.question: Is mean prediction confidence positively correlated across denoising steps with the number of early-decodable tokens as in Fig 1c?
follow_ups.method: Run LLaDA-1.5 draft inference on 15 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 128, logging per step the mean max-softmax confidence over the masked window and the number of positions whose current argmax equals the final greedy-decoded token as a proxy for early-decodable tokens. Compute the Pearson correlation between the two series across steps.

follow_ups.title: Tracking budget accuracy-throughput trade-off
follow_ups.question: Does increasing tracked-token budget beta_t improve accuracy but reduce throughput as in Fig 5a and Table 4?
follow_ups.method: Clone Flash-dLLM repo and run LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache plus Flash-Verify on 40 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 256, batch size 8, beta_m 64, epsilon 0.9, gamma 0.8, varying tracking budget beta_t over 48, 64, and 96. Report exact-match accuracy, tokens per second, and mean tokens accepted per step for each setting.

follow_ups.title: Verify threshold gamma trade-off
follow_ups.question: Does a higher Flash-Verify threshold gamma increase accuracy at the cost of throughput as in Table 4?
follow_ups.method: Using LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache plus Flash-Verify on 40 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 256, batch size 8, beta_t 64, beta_m 64, and epsilon 0.9, sweep verify threshold gamma over 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0. Report accuracy and throughput to test the predicted accuracy-throughput trade-off.

follow_ups.title: Flash-Verify versus confidence-aware decoding
follow_ups.question: Does Flash-Verify decode more tokens per iteration and give higher throughput than confidence-aware decoding at similar accuracy as in Fig 6?
follow_ups.method: Run LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache on 40 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 256 and batch size 8 under confidence-aware decoding with epsilon 0.9 versus Flash-Verify with epsilon 0.9 and gamma 0.8. Compare accuracy, throughput in tokens per second, and mean tokens decoded per iteration between the two strategies.

follow_ups.title: Masked-window size sweep
follow_ups.question: How does masked-window size beta_m affect accuracy and throughput for confidence-aware versus Flash-Verify decoding as in Fig 7?
follow_ups.method: Run LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache plus confidence-aware decoding and plus Flash-Verify on 30 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 256, batch size 8, beta_t 64, epsilon 0.9, gamma 0.8, varying beta_m over 16, 32, and 64. Measure accuracy and throughput for each window size and decoding method.

follow_ups.title: Batch-size throughput and memory scaling
follow_ups.question: Does Flash-dLLM throughput scale near-linearly with batch size while keeping peak memory low as in Fig 4?
follow_ups.method: Run LLaDA-1.5 with Flash-Cache plus Flash-Verify on 16 GSM8K 5-shot examples with generation length 256, beta_t 64, beta_m 64, epsilon 0.9, gamma 0.8, at batch sizes 1, 4, 8, and 16. Record throughput and peak GPU memory via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated for each batch size.

follow_ups.title: Generation-length throughput scaling
