follow_ups.method: Train one prefix autoencoder (D=512, TinyStories 64-token windows, Sec. 3.2 settings, ~3 minutes) and two block-causal x0-prediction denoisers (6 layers, hidden 512, rank-128 noisy-input projection, Q=8, tan-d d=5, EMA decay 0.999 given the short run, ~6 minutes each) that differ only in whether L_ct is added (warm-up over the first 20% of steps, S=16, stop-gradient through the state update and EMA target). For each model generate 300 samples with Euler at {4,8,16,32,64} steps, decode with the frozen decoder, and report GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL, entropy and MAUVE against held-out TinyStories windows per step budget, together with one-step x0 prediction error on held-out noisy latents at matched σ.

follow_ups.title: Exposure bias across blocks in block-causal latent generation
follow_ups.question: Training conditions every block on clean encoder prefixes while inference conditions on generated prefixes (Sec. 3.4–3.5); does decoded quality degrade with block index under free-running generation relative to teacher-forced (clean-prefix) generation, and is the degradation larger with smaller blocks, which the paper selects for higher MAUVE (Fig. 7b) but which require more sequential stages?
follow_ups.method: Train one prefix autoencoder (D=512, TinyStories 64-token windows, Sec. 3.2 settings, ~3 minutes) and two block-causal x0-prediction denoisers with Q=4 and Q=16 (6 layers, hidden 512, rank-128 noisy-input projection, tan-d d=5, two-stream mask, ~5 minutes each). For 300 held-out sequences, (i) free-run all blocks left to right with 16 Euler steps and (ii) for each block b generate only block b conditioned on the clean encoder prefix of the true sequence; decode both and report, as a function of b for each Q, the GPT-2 Large NLL of the decoded tokens of block b scored in the context of its (decoded or true) prefix, the repeated-token rate, and the fraction of degenerate blocks (e.g., all-EOS or a single repeated token).

follow_ups.title: Entropy-matched autoregressive frontier for the OpenWebText Gen-PPL/MAUVE comparison
follow_ups.question: Table 2 reports lower Gen-PPL for AURORA-LM-S than for the AR baseline (23.56 vs 39.40), but also lower token-unigram entropy (5.241 vs 5.605). Only AURORA-LM-S's sampler was tuned (a 30-setting sweep in Table 7); AR used Gumbel-max sampling with no reported tuning. At matched entropy, does an autoregressive model with the same backbone size reach comparable Gen-PPL and MAUVE with mildly sharpened sampling?
follow_ups.method: Generate 1,000 unconditional 1,024-token samples from GPT-2 small, whose 12-layer/768-hidden backbone matches the paper's AR baseline, starting from <|endoftext|> and not stopping at EOS, using vLLM or batched KV-cached sampling: temperature ∈ {1.0, 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8} at top-p 1, and top-p ∈ {0.95, 0.9} at T=1, with three seeds at T=1 and at the two settings whose entropy brackets 5.24; add GPT-2 medium at T=1 and at the bracketing settings as a reference nearer AURORA-LM-S's 267.8M total parameters. Score every set with GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL (exp of mean token NLL), mean per-sample token-unigram entropy in nats, and MAUVE against 1,000 held-out EOS-packed 1,024-token OpenWebText passages (gpt2-large features; final-layer last-token states can be reused from the Gen-PPL pass). Check that GPT-2 small at T=1 lands near the paper's AR row, then interpolate AR Gen-PPL and MAUVE at entropy 5.241 (AURORA-LM-S) and 5.155 (ELF-B) with seed-based uncertainty and compare with the reported rows, stating that this is a cross-harness comparison.

follow_ups.title: Chance and format-compliance floors of the generative two-shot benchmark protocol
follow_ups.question: By our arithmetic on Table 4, AURORA-LM-L's mean over the eight multiple-choice tasks (≈31.9) is at or slightly below uniform guessing (≈32.3). Cola-DLM's mean (≈25.0, with HellaSwag at 5.7) is well below it. The 32.6 vs 25.1 macro-average gap may therefore mostly reflect SQuAD exact match and answer parseability. Under the paper's exact protocol, what do trivial answer strategies and small open autoregressive models score, how often are outputs unparseable, and does the protocol rank models the same way log-likelihood scoring does?
follow_ups.method: Rebuild the Appendix A.2.9 protocol: labeled test split, else validation; seed-42 shuffle; ≤1,000 items per task; drop items whose Qwen3-tokenized two-shot prompt plus 32 new tokens exceeds 512, mimicking AURORA-LM-L's 512 positions; use the Table 17 demonstrations verbatim, greedy decoding of ≤32 tokens, first-newline truncation, normalization, and a strict matcher that accepts a lone option letter or the exact normalized option text and scores everything else wrong (report any task whose data cannot be loaded as missing). Score uniform-random, always-first, always-last and echo-the-option-list outputs, plus Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base via vLLM, reporting per-task accuracy with bootstrap 95% CIs, parse rate, accuracy among parsed outputs, macro averages with and without SQuAD, and the same models' log-likelihood multiple-choice accuracy. Re-score all outputs with a lenient substring matcher to measure how much matcher strictness alone moves per-task and average scores.

follow_ups.title: ROUGE implementation, subset and selection sensitivity for the XSum comparison
follow_ups.question: Table 3 places AURORA-LM-S's in-house ROUGE next to values quoted from the ELF paper, with margins of +0.6 ROUGE-1, +1.2 ROUGE-2 and +1.1 ROUGE-L. The paper does not state stemming, ROUGE-L variant or tokenization, and the setting selected in Table 8 reproduces the Table 3 numbers, which suggests selection and reporting used the same data. How large are the ROUGE shifts from these implementation choices, from subset sampling and from best-of-k selection, relative to those margins?
follow_ups.method: Produce XSum test summaries from two training-free systems: LEAD-1 (first article sentence) on the full test split, and Qwen3-1.7B in non-thinking mode prompted for a one-sentence summary (greedy, ≤60 tokens, vLLM), run on the full split with a default prompt and on a fixed 2,000-article subset with nine prompt/decoding variants. Score each output set under rouge_score with and without Porter stemming, ROUGE-L versus newline-split ROUGE-Lsum, raw versus lowercased/punctuation-stripped text, per-example mean versus bootstrap-aggregated mid F1, and the Hugging Face evaluate wrapper; report the max–min spread per metric and bootstrap 95% CI half-widths for random 1,000-example subsets and for the full split. Estimate selection optimism by picking the best of the nine variants on one random half of the subset and re-scoring it on the other half (100 random splits), and compare all three quantities with the reported margins.

follow_ups.title: Near-pure-noise coverage versus high-noise mass m0.7 as the driver of the noise-allocation effect
follow_ups.question: We recomputed high-noise mass from Eqs. 25–26. Mass above σ=0.9 orders the ten Table 14 schedules by MAUVE almost perfectly (Spearman ≈0.98), while the paper's m0.7 does not (≈0.88; logit-normal μ=1, s=0.5 has m0.7=0.62 but MAUVE 0.111). This is a post hoc pattern on ten single runs, and the best tan-d shift (d=7) was also the largest tested. Is generation quality governed by how much training covers near-pure-noise states rather than by m0.7, and does it keep improving beyond d=7?
follow_ups.method: Build a scaled-down replica of the paper's Sec. 3 pipeline on OWT128: GPT-2-tokenized 128-token OpenWebText chunks; one frozen prefix-aligned autoencoder with c=1, D=512, 4-layer causal encoder and decoder, p_x=0.3, p_z=0.6; and a block-causal clean-latent flow-matching denoiser (4–6 layers, hidden 384, two-stream mask, Q=16, D_b=64, no self-conditioning, consistency loss or guidance). Train six denoisers concurrently, each sized to reach ≥5k steps in about 8–10 minutes, differing only in training σ distribution: tan-d with d∈{7,15,30}; logit-normal μ=1, s=0.5; a 'no-tail' mixture 0.1·U(0,0.7)+0.9·U(0.7,0.9) (m0.7=0.90, m0.9=0); and a 'tail' mixture 0.7·U(0,0.7)+0.05·U(0.7,0.9)+0.25·U(0.9,1) (m0.7=0.30, m0.9=0.25). Sample all models on the same 32-step Euler grid (Eq. 13 update, tan-d d=7 spacing), 1,000 samples × 3 seeds, scoring MAUVE (gpt2-large features) against 1,000 held-out chunks, GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL and unigram entropy, and report Spearman correlations between MAUVE and m_{σ*} for σ*∈{0.5,0.6,…,0.95} on both the new runs and the paper's Table 14, treating tail versus no-tail as the decisive contrast and d=15/30 as a check on whether the optimum lies beyond d=7.

follow_ups.title: Isolating the active ingredient of self-trajectory consistency
follow_ups.question: Fig. 7a credits self-trajectory consistency with large few-step gains (MAUVE 0.116→0.672 at 8 steps) and attributes them to aligning clean-latent predictions along the model's own S=16 sampling trajectory. Do the gains remain if the neighbor state is built from the true clean latent, if the EMA target is taken at the same state, or if the consistency grid does not match the inference step count?
follow_ups.method: Build a scaled-down replica of the paper's Sec. 3 pipeline on OWT128: GPT-2-tokenized 128-token OpenWebText chunks; one frozen prefix-aligned autoencoder with c=1, D=512, p_x=0.3, p_z=0.6; and a 4–6-layer, hidden-384 block-causal clean-latent flow-matching denoiser (two-stream mask, Q=16, D_b=64, tan-d d=5, no self-conditioning or guidance, EMA decay 0.999 because runs are short). Train five denoisers concurrently for about 8–10 minutes each: (1) flow matching only; (2) plus the paper's consistency loss (t'=Prev_16(t) on the tan-d grid, Eq. 13 Euler step with stop-gradient own prediction, EMA target, λ_ct=1 with linear warmup); (3) a true-path variant whose neighbor state is (1−t')z+t'ε with the same ε; (4) a same-state variant whose EMA target is taken at (α_t,t); (5) the paper's loss built on a 64-step grid. Evaluate each at 8, 16, 32 and 64 Euler steps (1,000 samples × 2 seeds), reporting MAUVE (gpt2-large features vs 1,000 held-out chunks), GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL, unigram entropy and held-out flow-matching loss, so that few-step gains can be attributed to own-trajectory alignment versus generic regularization or reduced diversity.

follow_ups.title: Block size compared at matched numbers of sequential denoiser evaluations
follow_ups.question: Fig. 7b shows MAUVE falling from 0.909 (Q=4) to 0.631 (Q=64) at 32 steps per block. With N=128 latent positions, Q=4 then uses 1,024 sequential denoiser evaluations versus 64 for Q=64. Does the small-block advantage persist when total evaluations are matched, and does quality decay along the sequence as generated prefixes accumulate?
follow_ups.method: Build a scaled-down replica of the paper's Sec. 3 pipeline on OWT128: GPT-2-tokenized 128-token OpenWebText chunks; one frozen prefix-aligned autoencoder with c=1, D=512, p_x=0.3, p_z=0.6; and a 4–6-layer, hidden-384 block-causal clean-latent flow-matching denoiser (two-stream mask, D_b=64, tan-d d=5, no self-conditioning or guidance). Train three denoisers concurrently with Q∈{4,16,64} for about 10 minutes each, then sample 1,000 sequences × 2 seeds per model at 32 Euler steps per block and at matched totals of 256 and 1,024 sequential evaluations (Q=4: 8/32 steps per block; Q=16: 32/128; Q=64: 128/512). Score MAUVE (gpt2-large features vs 1,000 held-out chunks), GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL and unigram entropy, and also GPT-2 Large NLL per 16-token segment scored directly on the GPT-2 token ids given all preceding tokens, to see whether later segments degrade more with small or large blocks.

follow_ups.title: Causal prefix-aligned versus bidirectional autoencoder under block-causal and single-block denoising
follow_ups.question: The paper builds latents with a causal query encoder so that latent prefixes encode text prefixes, and argues this supports block-causal generation, but never compares against a bidirectional autoencoder. For unconditional generation, does prefix alignment improve quality, and does any benefit depend on block-causal (Q=16) versus single-block joint denoising?
follow_ups.method: Build a scaled-down replica of the paper's Sec. 3 pipeline on OWT128: GPT-2-tokenized 128-token OpenWebText chunks; c=1, D=512, 4-layer encoder and decoder, p_x=0.3, p_z=0.6; and a 4–6-layer, hidden-384 clean-latent flow-matching denoiser (D_b=64, tan-d d=5, no self-conditioning or guidance). Train two autoencoders of identical size concurrently for about 5 minutes: the paper's causal encoder with causal decoder, and a bidirectional encoder with bidirectional decoder. Then train four denoisers concurrently (each autoencoder × Q∈{16,128}, where Q=128 denoises the whole sequence as one block) and report: clean reconstruction accuracy; the paper's token-recovery-under-corruption curve (x_σ=(1−σ)z+σε on standardized latents, σ∈{0.1,…,0.9}, decoded without denoising); MAUVE of autoencoder reconstructions of held-out text as a ceiling; and MAUVE (gpt2-large features vs 1,000 held-out chunks), GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL and unigram entropy for 1,000 samples × 2 seeds. Use 32 steps per block for Q=16, and both 32 and 256 steps for Q=128 so total evaluations can be matched.

follow_ups.title: Width × latent-dropout ablation of the autoencoder
follow_ups.question: The autoencoder zeroes 60% of latent coordinates during training (p_z=0.6, no rescaling), which the paper never ablates. At fixed p_z, a wider latent retains far more surviving coordinates. Is latent dropout what makes generated latents decodable, and does the width advantage of Fig. 5 and Table 11 persist without it?
follow_ups.method: Build a scaled-down replica of the paper's Sec. 3 pipeline on OWT128: GPT-2-tokenized 128-token OpenWebText chunks; c=1, 4-layer causal encoder and decoder, p_x=0.3; and a 4–6-layer, hidden-384 block-causal clean-latent flow-matching denoiser (two-stream mask, Q=16, D_b=min(D,64), tan-d d=5, no self-conditioning or guidance). Train four autoencoders concurrently for about 5 minutes with D∈{64,512} × p_z∈{0,0.6}, freeze and standardize them, and train one denoiser per autoencoder with identical budgets. Report clean reconstruction accuracy, token-recovery-under-corruption curves (x_σ=(1−σ)z+σε on standardized latents, decoded directly), MAUVE of autoencoder reconstructions of held-out text as a ceiling, and MAUVE (gpt2-large features vs 1,000 held-out chunks), GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL and unigram entropy for 1,000 32-step samples × 3 seeds, estimating the width effect at each p_z and the width × dropout interaction with bootstrap CIs over sampling seeds.

follow_ups.title: Training-seed replication of the noisy-input bottleneck ablation
follow_ups.question: The case for D_b=128 (Fig. 6a, Table 13) rests on mean-MAUVE differences of about 0.02 (0.808 vs 0.790 without a bottleneck). These appear to come from single training runs (Table 6 lists one seed), and their sampling-seed SDs are 0.01–0.05. In this pipeline, how large is training-seed variance relative to sampling-seed variance, and does a low-rank noisy-input bottleneck still help once training-seed variability is included?
follow_ups.method: Build a scaled-down replica of the paper's Sec. 3 pipeline on OWT128: GPT-2-tokenized 128-token OpenWebText chunks; one frozen prefix-aligned autoencoder with c=1, D=512, p_x=0.3, p_z=0.6; and a 4–6-layer, hidden-384 block-causal clean-latent flow-matching denoiser (two-stream mask, Q=16, tan-d d=5, no self-conditioning or guidance). Train six denoisers concurrently for about 8–10 minutes: D_b=64 versus no bottleneck (a single D→H input projection), each with three training seeds and otherwise identical. Sample every model at 16, 32 and 64 Euler steps (1,000 samples × 2 seeds) and score MAUVE (gpt2-large features vs 1,000 held-out chunks), GPT-2 Large Gen-PPL and unigram entropy; then fit a two-level variance decomposition (training seed, sampling seed) and report the bottleneck effect with a CI that includes training-seed variability, stating whether it excludes zero rather than treating a null result as equivalence.

follow_ups.title: Wall-clock and evaluation-count cost of blockwise latent sampling versus autoregressive decoding
follow_ups.question: The paper weighs block size by the number of sequential stages but reports no latency. By our count, its OpenWebText configuration (Q=16 over 1,024 positions, 64 SDE-DPM++ steps, SC-CFG adding a second prediction per step) needs roughly 8,000 denoiser evaluations per sample, versus 1,024 for autoregressive decoding. On one A100 at matched backbone size, how does wall-clock generation time compare across block sizes, step counts, guidance settings and batch sizes?
follow_ups.method: Implement a randomly initialized 12-layer, 768-hidden block-causal denoiser (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE; D=768 noisy-latent input through a 128-dim bottleneck, full-width output) with KV caching of completed clean blocks, plus a 6-layer query decoder run once at the end. Time unconditional generation of 1,024 latent positions in bf16 for Q∈{4,16,64}, steps∈{16,32,64}, and guidance off or on (two predictions per step, batched), at batch sizes 1 and 64; weights do not affect timing. Also time the same 12-layer backbone decoding autoregressively with a KV cache and a 50,257-way output head, and Hugging Face GPT-2 small generate; report median wall-clock and evaluation counts over repeated runs, and pair each configuration with the quality the paper reports for it (Tables 2, 7 and 16, noting that Table 16 is at 128 tokens) to sketch a quality–latency frontier.

follow_ups.title: Prefix invariance under latent sequence compression
follow_ups.question: Does encoding a prompt alone produce the same latent prefix as encoding it within a longer sequence when N=round(cL)?
follow_ups.method: Implement the encoder and decoder visibility rules from equations 2–3 and a randomly initialized, frozen two-layer query encoder with width 128, using 512 OpenWebText passages tokenized to 128 tokens with GPT-2 BPE. For c in {1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7}, compare every shorter prompt encoded independently with its corresponding latent prefix from the full passage, then replace only the suffix and repeat. Report visible-token cutoff disagreements, numerical prefix changes, and whether positions treated as known during block-boundary repainting can access continuation tokens; this is an architectural audit, not a generation-performance test.

follow_ups.title: Latent width versus redundant coding
follow_ups.question: How much of wider latents' corruption robustness can be reproduced without adding information?
follow_ups.method: On 4,096 streamed OpenWebText documents and 512 document-disjoint held-out documents, use 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences to train two query autoencoders with identical two-layer, width-256 transformer trunks but learned latent projections of width 64 or 256, using 1,000 updates, batch 32, AdamW at 4e-4, and the paper's dropout probabilities. Construct a third condition by lifting the narrow standardized latent through a fixed 256-by-64 matrix R with R^T R=I, multiplying by two to match average per-coordinate signal variance, and decoding through R^T/2. Across two training seeds, measure token accuracy and reconstruction NLL at corruption levels {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9}, comparing both equal coordinate-noise levels and equal noise after inverse projection, with paired uncertainty intervals.

follow_ups.title: Gaussian corruption versus actual denoiser errors
follow_ups.question: Is robustness to isotropic Gaussian corruption a reliable proxy for robustness to the errors the latent prior actually makes?
follow_ups.method: Train a miniature pipeline on 4,096 OpenWebText documents with 512 document-disjoint held-out documents and 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences: two-layer query encoder and decoder with width 128, followed by a frozen representation and a two-layer endpoint-predicting denoiser with width 128, Q=8, and D_b=16, using 1,000 updates per stage, batch 32, and AdamW at 4e-4. At noise levels 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9 with true clean prefixes, collect prediction residuals r=predicted_z-z and compare decoding z+r against decoding z plus isotropic noise rescaled to exactly the same per-block residual norm, and against coordinate-permuted residuals. Repeat with two training seeds and report paired token accuracy and NLL relative to clean reconstruction, distinguishing held-out denoising errors from free-generation errors.

follow_ups.title: Does self-conditioning change the bottleneck result?
follow_ups.question: Does a narrow noisy-input pathway remain beneficial when full-width self-conditioning is removed?
follow_ups.method: Train and freeze one miniature query autoencoder with two layers per side and latent width 128 on 4,096 OpenWebText documents, using 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences, 1,000 updates, batch 32, and the paper's dropout probabilities, reserving another 512 documents for evaluation. Train four two-layer, width-128 denoisers crossing D_b in {16, 128} with self-conditioning probability in {0, 0.5}, keeping Q=8, full-width endpoint targets, tan-d shift 7, no consistency loss, and 1,000 AdamW updates at 4e-4 fixed, with three independent paired training seeds. Evaluate held-out error by noise bin and 256 generated sequences at 16 and 32 Euler steps, reporting entropy and MAUVE with fixed GPT-2 Large features and 16 buckets, plus training-seed uncertainty rather than treating sampling variation as evidence of equivalence.

follow_ups.title: Matched high-noise mass across schedule families
follow_ups.question: Is high-noise mass sufficient to explain generation quality, or does the shape of the training-time distribution matter?
follow_ups.method: Train and freeze a two-layer-per-side, width-128 query autoencoder on 4,096 OpenWebText documents with 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences, using 1,000 updates and batch 32, and reserve 512 document-disjoint documents for evaluation. Fit identical two-layer, width-128 denoisers with Q=8 and D_b=16 under tan-d shift 7 and two logit-normal schedules with s=0.5 or 1.0, choosing each mu using equation 26 so all three schedules have exactly the same probability of noise exceeding 0.7, with three paired training seeds and 1,000 updates per condition. Hold the 32-step Euler inference grid fixed across conditions and compare uniformly sampled noise-bin errors, entropy, and MAUVE from 256 generated sequences using GPT-2 Large features and 16 buckets, reporting differences and uncertainty rather than assuming matched mass implies equivalent schedules.

follow_ups.title: A controlled identifiability test for velocity prediction
follow_ups.question: Can a low-rank noisy-input pathway itself produce a clean-target advantage by hiding noise components needed for velocity prediction?
follow_ups.method: Generate standardized synthetic clean vectors of dimension 256 under both rank-32 and full-rank Gaussian covariance models, corrupt them with the paper's linear path and tan-d shift 7, and expose small GPU MLPs only to fixed rank-32 or full-rank projections of the noisy state. For three seeds and 500 updates per condition, compare direct clean prediction, raw velocity prediction evaluated in clean space, and residual velocity parameterization v=(x_t-g(projected_x_t,t))/t, keeping the clean-space loss weighting identical. Compare held-out errors with exact Gaussian conditional-mean bounds and verify the residual parameterization's gradient equivalence to clean prediction, treating this as a mechanism diagnostic rather than evidence about AURORA-LM's actual latent distribution.

follow_ups.title: Trajectory consistency versus generic EMA regularization
follow_ups.question: Does self-trajectory consistency improve few-step generation specifically because it uses a model-induced neighboring state?
follow_ups.method: Train and freeze a miniature two-layer-per-side, width-128 query autoencoder on 4,096 OpenWebText documents with 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences and 1,000 updates, then use two-layer denoisers with Q=8, D_b=16, tan-d shift 7, and self-conditioning probability 0.5. Compare flow matching alone, flow matching plus consistency against an EMA prediction at the identical noisy state, and the paper's model-induced neighboring-state consistency, giving each condition 90 seconds of GPU training for each of three paired seeds and using miniature-run EMA decay 0.99, consistency weight 1, a 100-update consistency warmup, and S=16. Record completed updates and evaluate 256 paired generations at 8, 16, and 32 Euler steps using entropy and MAUVE with GPT-2 Large features and 16 buckets, so trajectory-specific gains can be separated from generic EMA regularization under equal training-time budgets.

follow_ups.title: Decode–reencode projection of generated prefixes
follow_ups.question: Do generated prefixes drift away from encoder-produced latents, and does projecting them through the text interface help or harm subsequent generation?
follow_ups.method: Using 4,096 OpenWebText training documents, 512 held-out documents, and 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences, train two-layer, width-128 query autoencoders and denoisers for 1,000 updates per stage with batch 32, AdamW at 4e-4, c=1, Q=8, D_b=16, tan-d shift 7, self-conditioning probability 0.5, and no consistency loss or guidance. Across two training seeds, generate 256 paired sequences with 16 Euler steps per block, comparing ordinary latent-prefix conditioning with replacing each completed prefix by encode(argmax_decode(prefix)) and rebuilding its context cache. Measure standardized round-trip latent distance by block against the round-trip floor for held-out encoder-produced prefixes, record any edits to previously decoded tokens, and compare external GPT-2 Large perplexity, entropy, and MAUVE with 16 buckets.

follow_ups.title: Actual quality–latency trade-offs for block size
follow_ups.question: Is the selected block granularity attractive when complete inference latency, rather than just the number of sequential blocks, is measured?
follow_ups.method: Train one two-layer-per-side, width-128 query autoencoder for 1,000 updates on 4,096 streamed OpenWebText documents with 64-token GPT-2 BPE sequences, freeze it, and train three two-layer, width-128 endpoint denoisers with Q in {4, 16, 32}, D_b=16, tan-d shift 7, self-conditioning probability 0.5, and 1,000 updates each. Sweep 4, 8, and 16 Euler steps and self-conditioning guidance scales 1 and 4, checking cached predictions against uncached predictions before timing synchronized GPU inference at batch sizes 1 and 32, including decoding and counting every guidance evaluation. For 256 paired generated texts per setting, report full-system parameter counts, external GPT-2 Large perplexity, entropy, and MAUVE with 16 buckets alongside quality–latency Pareto curves, without assuming the miniature model's optimum transfers to the published model.

follow_ups.title: Benchmark answer-length and parsing stress test
follow_ups.question: Can context filtering, the 32-token answer cap, and output-format requirements depress measured multiple-choice accuracy independently of answer knowledge?
follow_ups.method: Construct the paper's Table 17 two-shot prompts for 200 deterministically selected public evaluation examples each from MMLU, HellaSwag, and RACE, tokenize with Qwen3, and measure context-budget exclusions plus whether correct option-text and option-letter oracle completions survive the 32-token and first-newline truncation rules. On retained prompts, run Qwen3-0.6B locally on the GPU with thinking disabled as a control, comparing free responses capped at 32 or 96 tokens with full-option likelihood ranking under identical prompts. Report valid-output rates, unconditional and valid-output-only accuracy, option-length effects, and paired uncertainty using an explicit letter-or-complete-option-text matcher, labeling this a protocol audit rather than a reproduction of undocumented parser details or a new AURORA-LM benchmark result.

follow_ups.title: Channel width versus latent count at fixed capacity
follow_ups.question: At equal latent scalar count, is it better to allocate capacity to wider channels or to more latent positions?
follow_ups.method: Use GPT-2 BPE and a two-layer mini-AURORA on 10,000 training and 1,000 held-out 128-token OpenWebText sequences; compare (D,N)=(64,128) with (128,64), using Q=16 and Q=8 so both have eight blocks and the same 8,192 latent scalars per sequence. Match update budgets and seeds, then compare held-out token cross-entropy, recovery over a Gaussian-corruption sweep, and 500-sample MAUVE and GPT-2 Large generation perplexity.

follow_ups.title: Causal prefix alignment versus full-context encoding
follow_ups.question: Does causal prefix alignment improve conditional continuation enough to justify its constraints on the autoencoder?
follow_ups.method: Train paired two-layer mini-AURORA systems on 10,000 OWT128 sequences; change only whether each encoder query sees its matching token prefix or the whole input, keeping query counts and decoder masks fixed. Freeze each autoencoder, train the same two-layer block-causal prior, and evaluate 32-token prompt continuations on 1,000 held-out sequences using prefix exact match, reconstruction cross-entropy, MAUVE, and GPT-2 Large generation perplexity.

follow_ups.title: Freezing versus joint autoencoder-prior training
follow_ups.question: Is freezing the autoencoder important for preserving a reliable text interface, or can joint adaptation make the latent prior easier to learn without harming decoding?
follow_ups.method: Pretrain a two-layer query autoencoder on 10,000 OWT128 sequences, then compare a prior trained with the autoencoder frozen against one that jointly updates the encoder, decoder, and prior using normalized token cross-entropy plus flow-matching loss. With matched data, seeds, and update budgets, compare held-out token cross-entropy, latent drift, clean-latent denoising error, and generated-text MAUVE and generation perplexity.

follow_ups.title: Exposure to generated latent prefixes
follow_ups.question: Does training block conditionals on clean prefixes create a measurable gap when earlier blocks are generated by the model?
follow_ups.method: Train a two-layer mini-AURORA prior on frozen OWT128 latents using the paper's parallel clean-prefix objective. On held-out sequences, score each next block with either the true encoded prefix or a prefix that starts with the same first block and is progressively replaced by model-generated blocks; report clean-latent error and decoded suffix cross-entropy by block index, plus free-running generation metrics.

follow_ups.title: Learned low-rank input versus fixed projection
follow_ups.question: Does the noisy-input bottleneck help because it learns which latent directions matter, or would any rank reduction have the same effect?
follow_ups.method: Train a two-layer autoencoder on 10,000 OWT128 sequences and freeze it; then train three priors on its D=128 latents, using a learned rank-32 noisy-input projection, a fixed random orthogonal rank-32 projection, or full-width noisy input. Keep the clean x0 target full-width and compare held-out denoising error by noise level and 500-sample MAUVE and generation perplexity.

follow_ups.title: Noise-schedule shape at matched high-noise mass
follow_ups.question: Does high-noise mass alone explain the schedule effect, or does the shape of the noise distribution matter when that mass is held fixed?
follow_ups.method: Train identical two-layer priors on the same frozen OWT128 latents using tan-d with d=5 and a logit-normal schedule whose mean is chosen to match its Pr(sigma>0.7); keep the model, update budget, and seeds fixed. Compare denoising error in noise-level bins and generated-text MAUVE and generation perplexity.

follow_ups.title: Testing the trajectory-specific consistency target
follow_ups.question: Does self-trajectory consistency help specifically by following the model's own Euler trajectory, rather than by matching predictions at nearby noise levels?
follow_ups.method: Train paired mini priors on frozen OWT128 latents with the same EMA target, consistency weight, S=16 schedule, and extra forward-pass budget; one uses the paper's model-predicted Euler-updated state, while the control uses the exact forward-path state at t' from the same clean-latent and noise pair. Compare prediction discrepancies and 8-, 16-, and 32-step generation using MAUVE and generation perplexity.

follow_ups.title: Block size quality-latency trade-off
follow_ups.question: Which block size provides the best practical balance between generation quality and sequential sampling cost?
follow_ups.method: Train separate two-layer priors on the same 10,000 OWT128 sequences with Q=4, 16, or 64, holding the denoiser size, training data, and update budget fixed. Generate 500 samples per model with 32 ODE steps per block; report MAUVE and generation perplexity alongside measured end-to-end latency and the number of sequential block stages.

follow_ups.title: Clean repainting for partial prompt blocks
follow_ups.question: When a prompt ends inside a latent block, does clean repainting preserve the known prompt while improving the generated continuation?
follow_ups.method: Train a two-layer conditional mini-AURORA on 5,000 XSum article-summary pairs, truncating sources to 128 GPT-2 BPE tokens and summaries to 32 tokens, with Q=8. On 500 held-out pairs, evaluate prompt lengths leaving each possible offset in the boundary block; compare clean repainting with denoising the entire boundary block, scoring source-prefix recovery and summary ROUGE by offset.

follow_ups.title: Parameter- and compute-matched autoregressive comparison
follow_ups.question: Does AURORA's free-generation advantage persist when the decoder and full training cost are counted?
follow_ups.method: Train a two-layer mini-AURORA and a two-layer autoregressive Transformer on the same OWT128 training sequences, using separate comparisons matched for active inference parameters and total training FLOPs; count the AURORA encoder, decoder, and denoiser in training cost and include the decoder in inference parameters. Generate 500 128-token samples per system and compare GPT-2 Large generation perplexity, MAUVE, unigram entropy, and measured sampling time.

follow_ups.title: Frozen autoencoder token recovery under increasing latent corruption
follow_ups.question: Does the released high-capacity autoencoder maintain accurate token decoding over a wide corruption range when corrupted latents are decoded directly without denoising?
follow_ups.method: Encode 200 OpenWebText sequences truncated to 128 tokens with the frozen AURORA-LM-S encoder from the repository linked in the paper and corrupt each latent sequence as interpolation between clean latent and Gaussian noise at six noise levels from zero to one. Decode all corrupted latents directly with the frozen decoder and report mean token-level recovery accuracy versus noise level.

follow_ups.title: Effective signal strength versus latent width and high-noise training mass
follow_ups.question: Does the effective per-dimension signal in the linear flow-matching path fall with larger latent width in a way that motivates heavier high-noise training allocation?
follow_ups.method: Encode 500 OpenWebText sequences of 128 tokens with the released AURORA-LM-S encoder, apply per-channel standardization from the paper, and compute mean squared latent norm and implied signal to noise ratio across noise levels. Compare the analytic high-noise mass above zero point seven for tan-d shifts one three five seven and logit-normal settings to link width-dependent signal dilution to the schedules that performed best in the paper.

follow_ups.title: Inference-time low-rank truncation of the noisy-input projection
follow_ups.question: Can the benefit of a narrow noisy-input bottleneck be probed at inference by truncating the input projection rank without retraining or changing the full-width clean target?
follow_ups.method: Take the released AURORA-LM-S denoiser with bottleneck width 128 and create rank-truncated variants at effective ranks 32 and 64 by singular value truncation of the fused input matrix while keeping the output head full width. Generate 60 short unconditional samples of 128 tokens per rank with 32-step ODE sampling without guidance and compare Gen-PPL from GPT-2 Large, unigram entropy, and MAUVE against shared held-out references.

follow_ups.title: Denoising-step budget and along-trajectory prediction stability at fixed weights
follow_ups.question: How do generation quality and successive-step clean-latent consistency degrade as the ODE step budget is reduced for a fixed checkpoint?
follow_ups.method: Generate 60 unconditional samples of 128 tokens per budget with the released AURORA-LM-S denoiser using deterministic ODE sampling at 8, 16, and 32 steps with block size 16 and no guidance. Score each budget with Gen-PPL, entropy, and MAUVE and log mean squared distance between consecutive-step clean-latent predictions on 20 trajectories to quantify error accumulation in the few-step regime.

follow_ups.title: Solver and self-conditioning guidance sweep for short-context free generation
follow_ups.question: Does SDE-DPM++ with stronger self-conditioning guidance lower Gen-PPL at matched steps relative to Euler ODE, and how does MAUVE respond?
follow_ups.method: Generate 50 unconditional samples of 128 tokens for each combination of solver in Euler and SDE-DPM++ with self-conditioning guidance scales 1 and 4 at 16 denoising steps using AURORA-LM-S. Score all four cells with Gen-PPL, entropy, and MAUVE using identical references and seeds to isolate solver and guidance effects on a small slice of the paper sweep.

follow_ups.title: XSum guidance and step selection on a small article subset
follow_ups.question: Do moderate classifier-free guidance and 32 ODE steps remain the best operating point for XSum ROUGE when evaluated on a small subset with the released checkpoint?
follow_ups.method: Encode 80 XSum source articles as clean latent prefixes with the frozen AURORA-LM-S encoder and generate summaries with 32-step ODE at guidance scales 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 plus a step sweep at 16, 32, and 64 steps with scale fixed at 2.0. Score each configuration with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L and report means and standard deviations over two sampling seeds.

follow_ups.title: Guidance application window for prompt-conditioned generation
follow_ups.question: Is restricting classifier-free guidance to the high-noise window sufficient for XSum quality compared with applying it over the full trajectory?
follow_ups.method: Generate summaries for 60 XSum articles with AURORA-LM-S using 32-step ODE and guidance scale 2.0 under three windows of no guidance and guidance in high-noise sigma in 0.9 to 1.0 and guidance at all steps. Compare ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L across windows at fixed seeds to test whether late-step guidance can be omitted without loss.

follow_ups.title: Inference-time block grouping beyond the training block size
follow_ups.question: Does the block-causal denoiser trained at block size 16 generalize to larger inference blocks that denoise more positions jointly with fewer sequential stages?
follow_ups.method: Generate 60 unconditional samples of 128 tokens with AURORA-LM-S using 32-step ODE without guidance while grouping positions into inference blocks of 16, 32, and 64 that are denoised jointly within each group and conditioned left to right across groups. Compare Gen-PPL, entropy, and MAUVE across group sizes to measure the quality parallelism tradeoff without retraining.

follow_ups.title: Partial-block prompt boundary handling for conditional generation
follow_ups.question: How sensitive is prompt-conditioned generation to the treatment of a prompt that ends inside a block?
follow_ups.method: Select 60 XSum articles whose encoded prompt lengths fall inside a 16-position block and generate summaries with AURORA-LM-S under three boundary rules of clean repainting of known positions and truncation to complete blocks only and generating the whole boundary block from noise. Use 32-step ODE with guidance scale 2.0 and compare ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L at fixed seeds.

follow_ups.title: Stability of generation metrics and few-shot answer matching under small samples
follow_ups.question: How stable are Gen-PPL, MAUVE, ROUGE, and few-shot accuracy to sample size, seed, and answer-parser choice when the evaluation budget is small?
follow_ups.method: Generate 200 short unconditional samples and 60 XSum summaries with AURORA-LM-S once and bootstrap subsamples of 50, 100, and 200 items over five resamples to report mean and spread of Gen-PPL, MAUVE, and ROUGE. Generate answers for 100 items each from two reasoning tasks with two-shot textual prompts and score each response twice with letter-only versus text-or-letter matching to quantify parser-induced shifts.

follow_ups.title: Query-aware routing versus strong fixed and task-only baselines
follow_ups.question: In a size-limited candidate pool, does query-aware routing improve on choosing the best model globally or separately for each task?
follow_ups.method: Cache batched, greedy responses from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 on 600 questions equally divided between ARC-Challenge and GSM8K, using disjoint, task-stratified 300/100/200 training/validation/test splits and output limits of 32/192 tokens respectively. Train cosine-kNN and 64-hidden-unit MLP selectors on frozen Contriever embeddings, selecting hyperparameters on validation data, and compare against every fixed candidate and validation-selected global and per-task fixed models. Report held-out accuracy, input/output token counts, diagnostic per-query oracle headroom, and paired task-stratified bootstrap intervals for routing gains.

follow_ups.title: Tie-breaking as a hidden source of router instability
follow_ups.question: Does assigning one best-model label when several models answer correctly make router performance depend on arbitrary candidate ordering?
follow_ups.method: Generate a cached response matrix for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 on 600 balanced ARC-Challenge/GSM8K questions with a fixed 300/100/200 training/validation/test split, batched greedy decoding, and respective 32/192-token output limits. Using frozen Contriever features and the same 64-hidden-unit MLP, compare cross-entropy against one arbitrarily selected correct model with cross-entropy against a uniform distribution over all correct models, excluding all-incorrect training rows from both conditions. Repeat across all six candidate tie-breaking priority orders and three initialization seeds, keeping model identities fixed, and report held-out accuracy differences with paired bootstrap intervals, selection distributions, and variability attributable to priority order.

follow_ups.title: Routing overhead and the measured quality–latency frontier
follow_ups.question: Do lightweight routers retain their apparent advantages when query encoding and routing latency are included?
follow_ups.method: On 320 balanced ARC-Challenge/GSM8K questions split 160/80/80 for training/validation/test, cache batched greedy answers of at most 192 tokens from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, then fit Contriever-based kNN and 64-hidden-unit MLP selectors alongside fixed-model baselines. Keep both LLMs and Contriever resident on the GPU, warm them up, and measure two repetitions of backend and routing stages at batch size one on 32 predetermined test queries, synchronizing the GPU around timings and including tokenization. Using validation-selected routing thresholds, compare accuracy–latency frontiers with routing overhead omitted versus included, and report paired timing intervals without converting local GPU measurements into hypothetical API prices.

follow_ups.title: Sensitivity to multi-agent role wrappers
follow_ups.question: Can semantically irrelevant role instructions change routing decisions even when the underlying question and candidate answers remain unchanged?
follow_ups.method: Cache batched greedy responses from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 on 512 balanced ARC-Challenge/GSM8K questions with 32/192-token answer limits and a 256/96/160 training/validation/test split, then train Contriever-based kNN and MLP selectors on canonical prompts. At test time, prepend only the Star-actor or Tree-worker role instructions from Appendix F.3 to the router input, keeping the complete question and cached backend responses unchanged, and compare full-prompt encoding against encoding only the original question. Report selection-flip rates, accuracy changes, and token-cost changes with paired bootstrap intervals and a query-independent baseline, explicitly treating this as an isolated template-sensitivity test rather than a full multi-agent evaluation.

follow_ups.title: Answer-option restrictions in multi-turn aggregation
follow_ups.question: How much aggregation error can arise from the paper's A–E output restriction when a question has ten answer options?
follow_ups.method: Select 100 ten-option MMLU-Pro questions and create two deterministic option permutations per question, placing the correct answer once within A–E and once within F–J, then cache batched greedy Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct specialist answers capped at 128 tokens using prompts that allow all ten options. Give identical specialist evidence to Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct aggregators using either Appendix F.2's A–E restriction or an otherwise identical A–J restriction, with greedy decoding capped at 32 tokens. Score every condition with the same A–J-capable parser and report accuracy, invalid-output rates, and paired changes by answer-position group with question-clustered bootstrap intervals.

follow_ups.title: Separating decomposer and aggregator capacity
follow_ups.question: Within a small multi-turn system, is performance more sensitive to the model that decomposes the question or the model that produces the final answer?
follow_ups.method: On 96 predetermined GSM8K test questions, run a 2×2 factorial experiment using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct independently as decomposer and aggregator, requesting exactly two subquestions and always using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the specialist. Use batched greedy decoding with limits of 96 tokens for decomposition, 128 per specialist answer, and 256 for aggregation; reuse each decomposition's specialist outputs across aggregators and add direct-7B and no-decomposition controls where each aggregator receives the same cached direct answer. Report final-answer accuracy, correction and corruption rates in the no-decomposition controls, every stage's tokens and GPU time, and paired bootstrap intervals for decomposer and aggregator effects.

follow_ups.title: Is draft verification worth its additional calls?
follow_ups.question: Does response-aware escalation improve model selection enough to justify its overhead compared with predicting the route from the question alone?
follow_ups.method: Cache batched greedy answers capped at 192 tokens from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for 480 balanced ARC-Challenge/GSM8K questions split 240/80/160 for training/validation/test. Compare a Contriever-based logistic predictor of 3B correctness with an AutoMix-style policy that first obtains the 3B draft and uses that same model's Correct/Incorrect verdict logits to decide whether to escalate, calibrating thresholds on validation data for target 7B-call fractions of 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. Evaluate both policies using identical cached backend answers and report accuracy, actual test escalation rates, all draft/verifier/escalation tokens, and fixed-batch GPU time with paired bootstrap intervals, rather than assuming equal escalation rates imply equal total cost.

follow_ups.title: Retrieval bottlenecks versus memory-routing headroom
follow_ups.question: Is poor performance on the memory track more attributable to missing retrieved evidence than to choosing the wrong answering model?
follow_ups.method: Sample 120 answerable LoCoMo questions across its conversations whose annotated evidence fits within five turn-pair chunks, reserve half for fixed-model selection and half for testing, and run Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with batched greedy answers capped at 48 tokens. Compare the paper's Contriever top-five retrieval condition with a diagnostic condition containing annotated supporting chunks plus retrieved distractors to reach five chunks, supplying identical contexts to both models. Report token-level F1, evidence coverage, context-token counts, the benefit of supplying annotated evidence, and the diagnostic per-query model-selection oracle gap relative to a validation-selected fixed model, using conversation-clustered bootstrap intervals.

follow_ups.title: Native-image routing versus caption-only routing
follow_ups.question: Does converting every image into a shared textual description remove useful opportunities to choose the input representation?
follow_ups.method: Using frozen Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on the GPU, compare native-image answering against image-only captioning followed by text-only answering with the same model on 240 multiple-choice MathVista examples, using identical images resized to at most 448 pixels on the longest side. Cap greedy captions at 160 tokens and answers at 96 tokens, and use an approximately 120/40/80 training/validation/test split grouped by shared image to train a question-only Contriever-kNN selector between the two paths. Report held-out accuracy against both fixed paths, diagnostic per-query oracle headroom, paired bootstrap intervals, and GPU time and token counts that include caption generation whenever the caption path is selected.

follow_ups.title: Stable persona signal versus judge artifacts
follow_ups.question: Do persona-conditioned preference labels contain reproducible user-specific information beyond response-order effects and judge-specific preferences?
follow_ups.method: Generate batched greedy responses capped at 160 tokens from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for all 80 first-turn MT-Bench questions, then have each model judge the anonymized pairs under the ten Figure 10 personas and a neutral condition in both response orders, limiting verdicts to eight tokens and never providing personas to answer generators. On a question-grouped 40/20/20 training/validation/test split, fit query-only and query-plus-persona logistic scorers using frozen Contriever features, an Elo baseline, and a control that independently shuffles persona identities within each training question, training and tuning only on 7B-judge labels. Report held-out agreement with both judges, personalization gains with question-clustered bootstrap intervals, tie and invalid-verdict rates, and order consistency, interpreting these as tests of synthetic preference stability rather than evidence of real-user benefit.

follow_ups.title: Headroom audit: per-query oracle and strongest fixed candidate versus the reported routers on xRouteBench
follow_ups.question: When the fixed-model baseline is the strongest single candidate selected on the training split (rather than the largest or smallest model), do learned routers still beat it on each track, and what fraction of the per-query oracle headroom do the reported routers actually capture?
follow_ups.method: Download the released xRouteBench query–model matrix (per-query task score and token cost for all 18 candidates, train and test splits) and, for every test set in Table 6, compute each candidate's mean test score and mean USD cost, the best fixed candidate chosen by training-split mean score (if no train split is available, choose it by 5-fold cross-validation on the test set and report both), the per-query oracle (max score over candidates, taking the cheapest candidate attaining it) and the oracle's mean cost. Place these next to the Table 2 router numbers and the Smallest/Largest/Elo rows to report, per track and on average, the router-over-best-fixed margin and the share of (oracle minus best-fixed) headroom each router recovers, flagging tracks such as LoCoMo where the oracle itself is close to the fixed baselines. No model inference is required.

follow_ups.title: Is Generic-track routing mostly task recognition? Subtask-identity routers versus query-level routers
follow_ups.question: How much of the gain of learned routers on the Generic LLM Tasks track (71–81 vs 70.29 for Largest-LLM in Table 2) is recovered by a router that only identifies which of the 13 source datasets a query comes from and sends the whole subtask to one candidate?
follow_ups.method: From the released xRouteBench Generic-track matrix (using its dataset/subtask field), build (i) a subtask-identity router that routes every test query of a subtask to the candidate with the highest training-split mean score on that subtask, (ii) the same router with the subtask predicted from query text by a logistic-regression classifier over all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings so no label is used at test time, and (iii) query-level kNN, SVM and MLP routers trained on the same embeddings with per-query best-candidate labels, plus the per-query oracle and the per-subtask oracle. Compare quality-only test accuracy overall and per subtask; if the subtask routers match the query-level routers, query-level modeling adds little beyond task identification. If the matrix is not released, build a local one by running Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct via vLLM on about 150 queries each from GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, MMLU, BoolQ and MBPP with the Appendix F.1 templates and a 70/30 train/test split.

follow_ups.title: Cost-aware routing by decision rule versus by retraining: one quality predictor with argmax(alpha*p_hat - beta*cost) against per-(alpha,beta) relabeled classifiers
follow_ups.question: Does a single per-candidate quality predictor combined with a cost-adjusted decision rule match or beat routers retrained at each of the five (alpha,beta) settings, and does the paper's finding that lightweight routers rise in rank under heavier cost weights persist under this rule?
follow_ups.method: On the released xRouteBench matrix, (a) fit once a per-candidate quality regressor (kNN neighbor-mean and a multi-output MLP over all-MiniLM-L6-v2 query embeddings) and route at each setting by argmax over candidates of alpha*p_hat_m - beta*c_hat_m, where c_hat_m is the candidate's training-split mean per-query cost normalized by the maximum per-query cost (also try per-track normalization and report both); (b) replicate the retrain approach by relabeling each training query with the candidate maximizing alpha*perf - beta*cost and refitting SVM/MLP classifiers and kNN votes separately for (1.0,0.0), (0.8,0.2), (0.6,0.4), (0.4,0.6) and (0.2,0.8). Evaluate weighted reward, mean performance and mean USD cost per track at every setting, plot both performance–cost frontiers against the per-query oracle frontier and the Smallest/Largest points, and report how the ranking of routers changes along the sweep under each mechanism.

follow_ups.title: Are Table 2's router rankings distinguishable from noise? Bootstrap and seed variability on xRouteBench
follow_ups.question: Given single-run numbers and test sets as small as 27, 61 and 100 queries, how often do router rankings per track, and the identity of the 'best average router', change under resampling of test queries and retraining with different seeds?
follow_ups.method: Re-implement kNN, SVM, MLP, matrix-factorization and Elo routers plus the Smallest/Largest rules on the released xRouteBench matrix (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, per-query best-candidate labels), train each learned router with 5 random seeds, and evaluate under the quality-only objective on 1,000 bootstrap resamples of every test set. Report per-router per-track 95% confidence intervals, the probability that each router is best on each track and best on the track average, and paired bootstrap p-values for all pairwise router differences; additionally compute analytic standard errors for the paper's reported single numbers (e.g., GMTRouter 68.78 vs PersonalizedRouter 67.86 on 308 queries, GraphRouter 42.62 vs EloRouter 45.90 on 61 Geometry3K queries) to state the smallest difference detectable at each test-set size.

follow_ups.title: Candidate-pool sensitivity: do router rankings and gains over the best fixed model survive changes to the pool?
follow_ups.question: Do the relative ranking of routers and their margin over the best fixed candidate persist when the 18-model pool is replaced by the 17-model no-cogito pool, a no-671B pool, a cheap-only pool (blended price at most $0.30 per 1M tokens in Table 9), or random 9-model subsets?
follow_ups.method: Using the released xRouteBench matrix, restrict the candidate columns to each pool, retrain kNN/SVM/MLP/MF/Elo routers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings) and evaluate per-track quality-only performance and the weighted objective at (alpha,beta)=(0.6,0.4), together with the best fixed candidate and the per-query oracle for each pool (10 random 9-model subsets, averaged). Report Kendall tau between the router ranking under the full pool and under each alternative pool, the router-over-best-fixed margin per pool, and the oracle performance lost by removing the expensive models, to determine whether the paper's conclusions are properties of the routers or of this particular pool.

follow_ups.title: Routing algorithm or sentence embedding: context-encoder ablation for kNN, SVM and MLP routers
follow_ups.question: Does swapping the off-the-shelf query embedding change absolute router performance and the ranking among kNN, SVM and MLP routers by more than the differences between these algorithms themselves?
follow_ups.method: Embed all xRouteBench train and test queries with locally runnable encoders of increasing strength — TF-IDF, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-base-en-v1.5 (or e5-base), Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B or -4B — plus a random-projection control, train kNN/SVM/MLP routers on each encoder's embeddings using per-query best-candidate labels from the released matrix, and evaluate on every track under the quality-only objective and at (alpha,beta)=(0.6,0.4). Report a routers-by-encoders table per track, compare the range of scores across encoders for a fixed router with the range across routers for a fixed encoder, and note whether the best encoder changes which router wins.

follow_ups.title: In-track versus cross-track supervision: transfer and negative transfer of routers across xRouteBench tracks
follow_ups.question: How much do router scores on the memory, vision and time-series tracks depend on in-track training data, and does adding Generic-track supervision cause negative transfer, as RouterDC's 16.39 on Geometry3K (below the smallest model's 27.87) suggests?
follow_ups.method: Train kNN/SVM/MLP/MF routers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, per-query best-candidate labels from the released matrix) under three regimes — Generic-only, in-track-only, and pooled Generic plus in-track — and evaluate each on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, Geometry3K, MathVista, Charades-Ego and TimeSeries under the quality-only objective, alongside Smallest/Largest, Elo, the in-track best fixed candidate and the per-query oracle. Report per-track scores for every regime, count how often cross-track-trained routers fall below the best fixed candidate, and relate each track's transfer gap to the cosine distance between its mean query embedding and the Generic track's mean embedding.

follow_ups.title: Does the persona change the verdict? Quantifying the personalization signal in persona-conditioned LLM-judge supervision
follow_ups.question: Using the paper's persona-judge prompt, how often does the preferred response flip when only the persona changes, compared with flips caused merely by swapping answer order, and do persona-conditioned model rankings differ materially from a persona-free ranking (which would explain why query- and user-independent EloRouter scores 66.40 vs 68.78 for GMTRouter)?
follow_ups.method: Collect about 300 prompt/answer-pair records (from the released xRouteBench personalized track if candidate responses are included; otherwise paired model responses from the public lmsys Chatbot Arena conversations dataset, or MT-Bench prompts answered by Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct) and judge each pair with a local 8B judge (Qwen3-8B with thinking disabled, served by vLLM) using the exact Appendix F.1 persona-judge template under 5 personas sampled from PersonaHub plus a no-persona control, each in both answer orders (about 3,600 one-token judgments). Report the position-consistency rate, the persona-flip rate after position debiasing, inter-persona Cohen's kappa versus inter-order kappa, Bradley–Terry model rankings per persona and their Spearman correlation with the persona-free ranking, and, where released DeepSeek-V3.1 labels or human Arena votes exist, agreement with them; if persona-induced disagreement is no larger than order-induced disagreement, the supervision carries little learnable personalization signal with this judge.

follow_ups.title: Why do multi-round routers collapse? Separating decomposition, aggregator capability and answer-format loss
follow_ups.question: Is the large deficit of decompose–route–aggregate routers (kNN-MultiRound 13.99 vs 57.55 for the smallest single model on Generic tasks) caused by harmful decomposition, by the weak Qwen2.5-3B aggregator, or by losing the task's answer format in the aggregation prompt?
follow_ups.method: On 80 queries each from GSM8K, ARC-Challenge and MBPP formatted with the Appendix F.1 templates, run with vLLM (routing fixed to a single specialist to isolate the other factors): (1) direct — Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct answers the query; (2) paper-style multi-round — Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct decomposes with the Appendix F.2 decomposition template, 7B answers every sub-query with the specialist template, and 3B aggregates with the general or multiple-choice aggregation template; (3) as (2) but with 7B as aggregator; (4) aggregate-only — no decomposition, the direct 7B answer is passed as the sole auxiliary information to the 3B aggregator; (5) MAS-style final node — the sub-answers from (2) are given to 7B as '[Team Analysis]' context together with the original task system instruction (Appendix F.3 shared final node). Score each condition with the task metric (answer match, choice accuracy, execution pass rate) and report the rate of unparseable outputs (missing <answer> tags or [BEGIN]/[Done] markers) per task and condition, plus generated tokens as a cost proxy.

follow_ups.title: Which nodes of a multi-agent system need the strong model? Position-based assignment rules versus uniform assignment in a Star topology
follow_ups.question: In a Star multi-agent system, is the benefit of per-node model choice concentrated at specific nodes (the final answer node, the planner), so that a simple position-based rule recovers most of the all-strong accuracy with a fraction of the strong-model calls?
follow_ups.method: Implement the Star topology from Appendix F.3 (planner decomposes into 3 subtasks, 3 actors solve them, planner consolidates, shared final node answers with the original task system instruction) over 150 queries from GSM8K and ARC-Challenge, using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as the weak model and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the strong model, both served by vLLM. Run the assignments all-weak, all-strong, strong only at the final node, strong at planner plus consolidation plus final node, strong only at the three actors, and single-call weak and strong without the MAS; report task accuracy with bootstrap confidence intervals, strong-model calls and generated tokens per query for each assignment, and test whether 'strong final node only' is statistically indistinguishable from all-strong.

follow_ups.title: Learned routers versus best-single-model, task-ID and oracle baselines on a small open pool
follow_ups.question: The paper's only fixed baselines pick the smallest or the largest model by parameter count. The abstract's 14.6% gain appears to be RouterDC (80.56) over Largest-LLM (70.29) on Generic LLM Tasks. The query-independent EloRouter averages 44.68 against 45.46 for the best router (Table 2). Against stronger simple baselines, namely the best single model chosen on training data and a router that knows only each query's source subtask, how much advantage do learned routers keep, and how much of the per-query oracle headroom do they capture?
follow_ups.method: Build a query–model matrix of correctness and cost (cost = (input+output tokens) × parameter count, normalized by the per-query pool maximum) for Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct (vLLM, greedy, ≤512 new tokens) on 200 queries each from MMLU, ARC-Challenge, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K and MBPP, using the paper's Appendix F.1 templates, one lenient answer extractor for all models, and execution of MBPP's asserts with a timeout. On a subtask-stratified 50/50 split, train kNN, SVM, MLP and bilinear matrix-factorization routers on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings for the weighted reward at (α,β) = (1,0) and (0.6,0.4), and compare them with Largest-LLM, Best-Single (best training reward), a Task-ID router (best training model per subtask), a cost-matched random mixture of two single models, and the per-query Oracle. Report test reward, accuracy and cost with paired-bootstrap 95% CIs for each router minus Best-Single and minus Task-ID, overall and per subtask, and repeat the router comparison with only 25 and 50 training queries per subtask.

follow_ups.title: Diagnosing the multi-turn collapse: decomposition, aggregator size, or answer-format mismatch
follow_ups.question: Multi-turn routers score 12.98–35.64 on Generic LLM Tasks versus 57.55 for Smallest-LLM (Table 2). The paper attributes this to decomposition and aggregation overhead and to the Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct base model. However, Appendix F.2's aggregation templates require <answer> tags, while the native Generic templates ask for a parenthesized letter or a step-by-step numeric answer. With sub-query answering held fixed, how much of the deficit comes from decomposition itself, how much from aggregator capacity, and how much from mismatch between the answer format and the extraction rule?
follow_ups.method: On 300 queries (100 each from MMLU, ARC-Challenge and GSM8K), run single-turn answers from Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct with the paper's native templates. Also run multi-round pipelines built from the paper's decomposition, specialist and aggregation templates, with decomposer/aggregator ∈ {Qwen2.5-1.5B, 3B, 7B-Instruct} and every sub-query answered by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, in three variants: aggregator alone (empty auxiliary information), undecomposed (the full query answered once by the 7B specialist and passed to the aggregator), and decomposed (≤4 sub-queries); use vLLM greedy decoding throughout. Score every output with both the strict native extraction used for single-turn answers and a lenient parser that reads <answer> tags first, and report accuracy, parse-failure rate and total token cost per variant with paired-bootstrap CIs.

follow_ups.title: How persona-specific are persona-conditioned judge labels?
follow_ups.question: The personalized track's labels come from a judge conditioned on a PersonaHub persona that the candidates never see. The user-agnostic EloRouter is within 2.4 points of the best personalized router (66.40 vs. 68.78, Table 3). Using the paper's persona-judge prompt with an open 7B judge (not the paper's DeepSeek-V3.1, so this tests the protocol rather than the released labels), how much of the variation in pairwise verdicts is persona-specific (persona × item) rather than persona-invariant quality, and how does that compare with the judge's own inconsistency when answer positions are swapped?
follow_ups.method: Generate answers (vLLM, greedy, ≤384 new tokens) to the 80 MT-Bench first-turn questions (FastChat llm_judge question.jsonl) with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Phi-3.5-mini-instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, and sample 3 response pairs per question (240 pairs). Judge every pair in both presentation orders with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using the paper's persona preference template, under 10 random personas from proj-persona/PersonaHub plus a no-persona control, reading P('1'), P('2') and P('Tie') from first-token log-probabilities. Report position consistency; how often each persona's order-debiased verdict differs from the no-persona verdict, overall, by MT-Bench category and by the pair's no-persona preference margin; and a variance decomposition of P(answer A preferred) into item, persona, persona × item, order and order × item components.

follow_ups.title: Are cross-track router winner changes distinguishable from sampling noise?
follow_ups.question: The 'no single router dominates' finding rests partly on tracks with 27–127 test queries (Table 6). At those sizes one query moves accuracy by 0.8–3.7 points, and the paper reports no confidence intervals or repeated splits. How often do the top router and the router ranking change between two disjoint test samples of the same size drawn from the same task? Do winners differ between tasks more often than this within-task noise baseline?
follow_ups.method: Build a correctness matrix for Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct (vLLM, greedy, ≤512 new tokens) on 400 queries each from MMLU, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA and GSM8K with the paper's templates. Train kNN, SVM, MLP and matrix-factorization routers on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, alongside a Best-Single baseline, over five random 40/60 train/test splits. Within each subtask, draw 1,000 pairs of disjoint test subsamples of size n ∈ {27, 61, 100, 120} and record top-router agreement and Kendall's τ; compare these with how often the top router differs between subtasks at the same n, and report ranking variation across the five splits and across the five leave-one-model-out pools. Separately, compute exact binomial 95% CIs for the paper's accuracy-type Table 2 entries (Geometry3K, MathVista, Video, TimeSeries) at their Table 6 sizes.

follow_ups.title: Cost-weighted rank reversals: router design or label construction?
follow_ups.question: Figure 5 shows large rank shifts as the cost weight β grows: RouterDC falls from first to tenth of eleven on Generic LLM Tasks, and MLPRouter is best on Vision for β ≥ 0.4. The paper does not describe how cost is normalized or how ties among equally correct candidates are broken when per-weighting training labels are formed. Do such reversals persist when the β = 0 tie-breaking rule is varied? Do they persist when retraining for each weighting is replaced by one per-model correctness predictor combined with a cost-aware decision rule applied at test time?
follow_ups.method: Build a matrix for Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct (vLLM, greedy, ≤512 new tokens) on 200 queries each from MMLU, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA and GSM8K. Use cost = (input+output tokens) × parameter count, normalized by the per-query pool maximum and, as a sensitivity check, by the global maximum. For each of the paper's five (α,β) weightings, train kNN, SVM and MLP classifiers on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings to predict argmax_m α·perf − β·cost (at β = 0, under cheapest-, random- and first-listed tie-breaking), and compare them with a single logistic per-model correctness predictor whose test-time rule is argmax_m α·p̂ − β·ĉ, where ĉ is the per-model mean training cost. Report test reward per weighting, area under the accuracy–cost curve, training-label entropy per weighting, and Spearman correlation of router rankings across weightings, with paired-bootstrap CIs.

follow_ups.title: Annotator-conditioned preference routing on real human votes, with a permuted-ID placebo
follow_ups.question: The paper's real-user evidence (Table 4) comes from 8 held-out Slack sessions. There, PersonalizedRouter (83.05) and the user-agnostic EloRouter (82.20) differ by under one point, and the persona-judge winner, GMTRouter, falls to sixth. On a larger public set of real pairwise votes that records annotator identity, does conditioning on the annotator improve held-out preference prediction beyond global and query-aware models? Does any such gain exceed what randomly permuted annotator IDs produce?
follow_ups.method: Load the expert human judgments released with MT-Bench (lmsys/mt_bench_human_judgments, 'human' split: question, turn, model pair, winner, annotator 'judge' field). Using 5-fold cross-validation over questions, fit L2-regularized Bradley–Terry logistic models with (i) global model strengths (an EloRouter analog), (ii) (i) plus model × MT-Bench-category interactions (categories from FastChat question.jsonl) and model × all-MiniLM-L6-v2 query-embedding interactions, (iii) (ii) plus per-annotator model offsets, and (iv) model (iii) refit 20 times with annotator IDs randomly permuted. Score held-out records by pairwise selection accuracy (tie = 0.5, as in the paper) and log-loss; report question-level bootstrap CIs for (iii) − (ii) against its placebo distribution, and show the spread of accuracy differences between models when test sets are subsampled to about 50 records, roughly the size of the paper's 8-session Slack test split.

follow_ups.title: Per-node versus per-query routing in a multi-agent Chain topology
follow_ups.question: Table 5 reports that routing every node of a multi-agent system beats always using Largest-LLM (best average 76.48 vs. 71.48). It has no per-query-routing or best-single-model baseline, and every Table 5 average is below the best single-turn Generic LLM Tasks score in Table 2 (80.56; Table 5 may use a subset of the split). Does the gain come from assigning different models to different node roles, or from routing as such? Does the multi-agent system beat single-turn routing at all?
follow_ups.method: Build a correctness matrix for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (vLLM, greedy, ≤512 new tokens, all three loaded on the GPU at once) on 600 training queries from MMLU, ARC-Challenge, CommonsenseQA and GSM8K, and train a kNN router on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings with cheapest-correct-model labels. On 200 held-out queries, run the paper's Chain topology (Appendix F.3 templates plus the shared final node, 4 calls) under four conditions: each fixed model at every node; per-query routing (route the user query once and reuse that model at every node); per-node routing (route each node's full prompt); and uniformly random per-node assignment. Also run single-turn answering by each model and by the kNN router, and report accuracy and token cost per condition with paired-bootstrap CIs, plus the distribution of selected models by node role.

follow_ups.title: Context encoder versus scoring rule: which router component drives routing quality, in and out of distribution?
follow_ups.question: The paper motivates its five-component formulation by the difficulty of isolating which design elements drive performance. It says component ablations need only a one-line change, but it reports none. With data and candidate pool fixed, does the context encoder E_q or the scoring/decision rule (g, d) explain more of the variation in routing accuracy? Does this change when the test subtask is unseen during training?
follow_ups.method: Build a correctness matrix for Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct (vLLM, greedy, ≤512 new tokens) on 200 queries each from MMLU, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA, HellaSwag and GSM8K with the paper's templates. Cross four encoders (TF-IDF, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-base-en-v1.5, mean-pooled last-layer states of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) with four scorers (kNN vote; SVM and MLP classifiers on cheapest-correct labels; per-model logistic correctness predictors with argmax), and evaluate every pair on three random 50/50 splits and in six leave-one-subtask-out folds. Report accuracy for all 16 pairs, a two-way variance decomposition into encoder, scorer and interaction for each regime, and paired-bootstrap CIs against Best-Single chosen on the training subtasks.

follow_ups.title: Is memory-track routing headroom capped by retrieval recall?
follow_ups.question: On LoCoMo, every router and both rule-based baselines fall within 24.49–27.64 token-F1 (Table 2), under a fixed top-5 Contriever retrieval over turn pairs (Appendix A.2). Is this flatness explained by retrieval misses that no candidate can overcome? If so, differences between models and oracle-routing headroom should appear only when the evidence is in context.
follow_ups.method: From LoCoMo (git clone snap-research/locomo; data/locomo10.json), take about 600 non-adversarial QA items (category ≠ 5). Build adjacent turn-pair chunks with speaker and date, retrieve with facebook/contriever as in Appendix A.2, and compute evidence recall@5 and recall@20 from the annotated evidence dialogue IDs. Answer every item with Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct (vLLM, greedy) using the paper's LoCoMo prompt under three contexts (top-5 retrieved, top-20 retrieved, gold evidence), and report token-F1 per model, per-query oracle-routing F1, and the between-model F1 spread split by retrieval hit versus miss, with bootstrap CIs.

follow_ups.title: Do caption-rendered vision queries measure visual reasoning, and do routing labels depend on the captioner?
follow_ups.question: The vision track replaces each image with a single Gemma-3-27B-IT description and routes text-only queries (Appendix A.4). Routing labels could therefore reflect captioner quality, text priors in the question, or answers leaked into captions, rather than candidates' reasoning about the figure. How much does candidate accuracy depend on the caption? Do model rankings and per-query best-candidate labels change when a different, smaller open captioner is used?
follow_ups.method: On 300 MathVista testmini items (AI4Math/MathVista; multiple-choice and integer-answer items only), generate descriptions with the paper's image-captioning prompt using Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, with image resolution capped. Have Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct answer with the paper's visual-math prompt under no-caption, 3B-caption and 7B-caption conditions (vLLM, greedy), and have Qwen2.5-VL-7B answer from the raw image as a reference. Report accuracy per candidate and condition, agreement of model rankings and of per-query best-candidate labels across caption sources (Cohen's κ), oracle-routing headroom per condition, and, as a crude leakage check, how often captions contain the gold answer string, with bootstrap CIs.

follow_ups.title: Routing gains against strong fixed-model baselines
follow_ups.question: Does query-aware routing improve on learning the best global or per-task model?
follow_ups.method: Locally generate batched, deterministic responses from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 on question-disjoint 40/20/40 training/validation/test samples from each of ARC-Challenge, GSM8K and MMLU-Pro, using complete option lists, task-correct answer alphabets, and 32-token multiple-choice or 192-token math caps.
